description: Two quantum particles are entangled if measuring one instantly affects the other. But entanglement is also a topological property: if you represent the state of two qubits as a curve in R^3, entanglement IS the linking number. Conjecture: For any pure state of two qubits |psi> in C^2 tensor C^2, the concurrence C(psi) = 2|alpha*delta - beta*gamma| (where psi = alpha|00> + beta|01> + gamma|10> + delta|11>) equals the absolute value of the linking number of two curves derived from the Hopf fibration applied to psi. Specifically, map psi to S^7 via normalization, then project to S^4 via the Hopf map, and the preimages of two points in S^4 are linked circles in S^7 whose linking number equals the concurrence. This means: entanglement is MEASURED by topology, and maximally entangled states correspond to the Hopf link (linking number 1). Test: for 1000 random two-qubit states, compute the concurrence and the linking number of the Hopf preimages, and verify they are equal. Prove the equality for the Bell states. Impact: quantum entanglement is not mysterious — it is the linking number of the Hopf fibration. Two particles are entangled if and only if their Hopf preimages are linked.
proof_strategy: Define the Hopf fibration: S^3 -> S^2 by (z1, z2) -> (2*z1*z2_bar, |z1|^2 - |z2|^2). For a two-qubit state psi = alpha|00> + beta|01> + gamma|10> + delta|11>, define the reduced state rho_1 = Tr_2(|psi><psi|). The concurrence is C = 2|alpha*delta - beta*gamma|. Map: given psi, form the complex matrix M = [[alpha, beta], [gamma, delta]]. The concurrence equals 2|det(M)| = 2|alpha*delta - beta*gamma|. Now the Hopf linking: consider the curves gamma_1(t) = (alpha*e^{it}, beta) / ||(alpha*e^{it}, beta)|| and gamma_2(t) = (gamma*e^{it}, delta) / ||(gamma*e^{it}, delta)|| in S^3. The linking number of gamma_1 and gamma_2 in S^3 equals |det(M)| (by the Whitehead formula for linking in S^3). Therefore C = 2 * |linking number|. Normalizing: C/2 = |linking number|, so the normalized concurrence equals the linking number. For Bell states: |Phi+> = (|00>+|11>)/sqrt(2) has alpha=delta=1/sqrt(2), beta=gamma=0, C=1, linking number=1. For product states: |00> has C=0, linking number=0. Test: verify for 1000 random states.
title: Quantum Entanglement as Algebraic Topology: The Linking Number Is Entanglement

description: In 2023, Smith et al. discovered 'the hat' — a single tile shape that tiles the plane but only aperiodically (no periodic tiling exists). This solved the aperiodic monotile problem. But deeper questions remain: How many distinct aperiodic monotiles exist? Conjecture: The set of aperiodic monotiles forms a 1-parameter family (the 'hat spectrum') parameterized by a continuous parameter t in [0,1] where t=0 gives the hat, t=1 gives the turtle (a known variant), and intermediate values give intermediate shapes. The key property: each shape in the hat spectrum tiles the plane aperiodically, and no two shapes in the spectrum admit a common periodic tiling. The boundary of the hat spectrum is the curve in R^2 that separates the region of aperiodic monotiles from the region of periodic tiles. This boundary is a piecewise-smooth curve determined by the constraint that the tile must enforce a hierarchical substitution rule. Test: parameterize the hat spectrum by interpolating between the hat and turtle, compute the substitution rule for each t, and verify that the substitution rule enforces aperiodicity for all t in [0,1]. Impact: aperiodic monotiles are not isolated curiosities — they form a continuous family, and the hat is just one point on the spectrum.
proof_strategy: Define the hat spectrum: for t in [0,1], the tile H_t is the convex hull of the 14 vertices of the hat tile with one edge parameterized by t. At t=0, H_0 is the hat. At t=1, H_1 is the turtle. For intermediate t, H_t is the interpolated shape. The substitution rule for H_t is a function of t: the tile H_t admits a substitution rule with expansion factor lambda(t) where lambda(0) = sqrt(3) + 2 (the hat expansion factor) and lambda(1) = sqrt(3) + 2 (the turtle expansion factor, same as the hat). Actually lambda(t) = sqrt(3) + 2 for all t because the substitution rule is the same hierarchical rule parameterized by t. Prove aperiodicity: for each t in [0,1], the substitution rule for H_t forces a hierarchical tiling that is aperiodic (no translational symmetry). The key argument: the substitution forces a pattern of 'meta-tiles' at each scale, and the meta-tile pattern at scale n determines the tile pattern at scale n+1 uniquely. A periodic tiling would require a scale at which the meta-tile pattern has translational symmetry, which contradicts the forced hierarchy. Test: implement the substitution rule for H_t for t = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 and verify each produces an aperiodic tiling.
title: The Aperiodic Monotile: One Shape to Tile Them All

description: The Langlands program connects Galois groups (shapes) to automorphic forms (colors). Think of it this way: a Galois group is the group of symmetries of a shape (like the rotational symmetries of a polygon). An automorphic form is a coloring that respects the shape's symmetries (like a coloring of the polygon's vertices that is invariant under rotation). The Langlands correspondence says: for every 'shape' (Galois representation), there is a matching 'color' (automorphic form) and vice versa. Conjecture: This correspondence is a bijection between irreducible representations of Gal(Q_bar/Q) and cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over Q. For n=1, this is class field theory (every abelian extension of Q corresponds to a Dirichlet character). For n=2, this is the modularity theorem (every elliptic curve over Q corresponds to a weight-2 cusp form). The toddler version: each shape has exactly one matching color, and each color has exactly one matching shape. Test: verify the correspondence for all degree-2 extensions of Q up to discriminant 1000. Verify that each quadratic field Q(sqrt(d)) corresponds to a Dirichlet character chi_d via the correspondence chi_d(p) = (d/p) (Legendre symbol). Impact: Langlands is just shape-color matching. Shapes and colors are two ways of seeing the same mathematical object.
proof_strategy: State the Langlands correspondence for GL_2: there is a bijection between irreducible 2-dimensional Galois representations rho: Gal(Q_bar/Q) -> GL_2(C) and cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_2 over Q. For the toddler version: every quadratic field Q(sqrt(d)) corresponds to a Dirichlet character chi_d: (Z/DZ)* -> {±1} where D is the discriminant. Verify: for d = -1 (Q(i)), D = -4, chi_{-4}(n) = (-1)^{(n-1)/2} for odd n. For d = 2 (Q(sqrt(2))), D = 8, chi_8(n) = (-1)^{(n^2-1)/8}. For each d with |d| < 1000, compute the Dirichlet character chi_d and verify it matches the splitting behavior of primes in Q(sqrt(d)): p splits iff chi_d(p) = 1, p is inert iff chi_d(p) = -1, p ramifies iff p | D. This is the Kronecker-Weber theorem for quadratic fields, which is the n=1 case of Langlands. For n=2, verify the modularity theorem: every elliptic curve E over Q with conductor N has an associated cusp form f_E in S_2(Gamma_0(N)) such that a_p(E) = a_p(f_E) for all primes p. Test: verify for curves in the Cremona database up to conductor 1000.
title: Langlands for Toddlers: Galois Groups as Shapes, Automorphic Forms as Colors

description: The Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has zeros at the non-trivial points s = 1/2 + i*gamma_n where gamma_n are the imaginary parts of the zeros. The Fourier transform of the zero counting function N(t) = #{gamma_n <= t} is related to the distribution of primes by the explicit formula. But what if we take the Fourier transform of zeta itself? Define Z(t) = zeta(1/2 + it) as a function of the real variable t. The Fourier transform Z_hat(w) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} Z(t) * e^{-2*pi*i*w*t} dt. Conjecture: Z_hat(w) has sharp peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi for each prime p. This is because the explicit formula expresses zeta(1/2+it) as a sum over primes: zeta(1/2+it) ~ sum_{p} p^{-1/2-it} = sum_{p} e^{-it*log(p)} / sqrt(p), which is a sum of complex exponentials with frequencies log(p). The Fourier transform of a sum of exponentials is a sum of delta functions at the frequencies log(p)/2*pi. So Z_hat(w) = sum_{p} delta(w - log(p)/2*pi) / sqrt(p) + (error from zeros and smooth terms). The peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi give a 'spectrogram' of the primes. Test: compute Z_hat(w) numerically for the first 10^6 zeros and verify the peaks at log(2)/2*pi, log(3)/2*pi, log(5)/2*pi, etc. Impact: you can HEAR the primes by playing the Fourier transform of the Riemann zeta function — each prime is a distinct note.
proof_strategy: Define Z(t) = zeta(1/2 + it) for real t. The Fourier transform Z_hat(w) = integral Z(t) e^{-2*pi*i*w*t} dt. By the explicit formula: zeta(1/2+it) = sum_{p} p^{-1/2-it} + (terms from zeros and smooth parts). The prime sum = sum_p e^{-it*log(p)} / sqrt(p). Fourier transform of e^{-it*log(p)} is delta(w - log(p)/2*pi). So Z_hat(w) = sum_p delta(w - log(p)/2*pi) / sqrt(p) + (smooth error). The error terms come from: (1) the trivial zeros at s = -2n, contributing e^{-2*pi*i*w*2n} = delta(w = n), (2) the non-trivial zeros, contributing a smooth background, (3) the logarithmic derivative of the gamma factor. The key insight: the peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi are SHARP (delta-function-like) because there are infinitely many zeros that reinforce these frequencies. Compute numerically: evaluate Z(t) for t in [0, T] with step dt, compute FFT, and look for peaks at w = log(2)/2*pi ≈ 0.110, log(3)/2*pi ≈ 0.174, log(5)/2*pi ≈ 0.256, etc. Test: verify peaks at these frequencies using the first 10^6 zeros with T = 10^6.
title: The Fourier Transform of the Riemann Zeta: Hearing the Primes

description: The primes have density 0 in the integers, but what is the Hausdorff dimension of the set of primes viewed as a subset of R? Define the 'prime fractal' P as the set of primes with the metric d(p,q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|. This metric stretches out the primes so that the twin primes are close together and the large primes are spread out. Conjecture: The Hausdorff dimension dim_H(P, d) = 1. The primes with this metric are essentially a 1-dimensional set — they fill out a line when viewed through the logarithmic lens. This is because the prime number theorem pi(x) ~ x/log(x) means that in the d-metric, the 'length' of the primes up to x is sum_{p <= x} d(p, p+1) ~ sum_{p <= x} 1/(p*log(p)) ~ log(log(x)), which diverges. So the primes are 'long enough' to be 1-dimensional. But the Hausdorff dimension might be > 1 if the primes have fractal structure at small scales. In fact, dim_H(P, d) > 1 would mean the primes are more than a line — they have 'wrinkles' that fill more space. The twin prime conjecture predicts that there are infinitely many pairs of primes at d-distance ~ 1/(p*log(p)), creating a fractal dust that increases the dimension. Conjecture: dim_H(P, d) = 1 + epsilon where epsilon depends on the density of twin primes. If the twin prime conjecture is true, epsilon > 0. Test: estimate dim_H(P, d) by box-counting for primes up to 10^12 and verify it is close to 1 (or slightly above). Impact: the primes are a fractal with dimension 1 + epsilon, where epsilon measures the abundance of twin primes. If twin primes are infinite, the primes are more than a line — they are a fractal curve.
proof_strategy: Define the metric d(p, q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)| on the set of primes P. Compute the Hausdorff dimension: dim_H(P, d) = lim_{delta -> 0} inf{sum r_i^s : P covered by balls of radius r_i < delta} where s is the infimum such that the sum is finite. By the prime number theorem, the interval [2, x] contains pi(x) ~ x/log(x) primes, and the d-length of this interval is 1/log(2) - 1/log(x) ~ 1/log(2). The 'average spacing' in the d-metric between consecutive primes near p is ~ 1/(p*log(p)^2). The box-counting dimension: N(epsilon) ~ (1/log(2)) / epsilon * (1/log(1/epsilon)) (number of boxes of size epsilon needed to cover P). So dim_box(P, d) = lim_{epsilon->0} log(N(epsilon))/log(1/epsilon) = 1 (since the log(1/epsilon) factor is sub-polynomial). For the Hausdorff dimension: if twin primes are infinite, the set of twin primes has accumulation points that may increase dim_H above 1. The key: the set of twin primes with the d-metric has dimension dim_H(twin primes, d) = 1/2 (since twin primes have density ~ C_2 * x/(log(x))^2 which gives s-measure finite for s > 1/2 and infinite for s < 1/2). So dim_H(P, d) = max(1, 1/2) = 1. The twin primes add a set of dimension 1/2 which does not increase the overall dimension. Conjecture: dim_H(P, d) = 1 exactly. Test: compute box-counting dimension numerically.
title: Fractal Number Theory: Hausdorff Dimension of Prime Distributions

description: The Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has non-trivial zeros at s = 1/2 + i*gamma_n on the critical line (assuming RH). These zeros encode deep arithmetic information. Conjecture: the zeros gamma_n are the spectrum of a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space, and this operator is the Casimir element of a quantum group G_q. Specifically, define the 'zeta quantum group' G_q as the q-deformation of SU(2) where q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1} (using the first zero gamma_1 ~ 14.13). The Casimir element C_q of G_q has eigenvalues that are quadratic functions of the representation labels, and the spectrum of C_q is {n(n+1) : n in N}. Conjecture: the Riemann zeros gamma_n are related to the spectrum of C_q by gamma_n = f(spectrum(C_q)) for some function f. If f is linear, this would mean the zeros are evenly spaced, which is false (the zeros have Poisson-like spacings). If f is logarithmic, gamma_n ~ pi*n/log(n) which matches the average spacing. Conjecture: the spectral statistics of C_q match the GUE random matrix statistics of the Riemann zeros (Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture). Test: compute the spectrum of C_q for G_q with q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1} and compare the spectral statistics with the Riemann zeros. Impact: the Riemann hypothesis is a representation-theoretic statement about quantum groups.
proof_strategy: Define the quantum group SU_q(2) with q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1} where gamma_1 ~ 14.13 is the first Riemann zero. The representation theory: irreducible representations V_n of dimension n+1 for n = 0, 1, 2, .... The Casimir element C_q acts on V_n with eigenvalue [n]_q * [n+1]_q where [m]_q = (q^m - q^{-m})/(q - q^{-1}) is the q-integer. For q = e^{2*pi*i*gamma_1}: [m]_q = sin(m * pi * gamma_1) / sin(pi * gamma_1). The eigenvalues of C_q on V_n are: lambda_n = [n]_q * [n+1]_q = sin(n*pi*gamma_1) * sin((n+1)*pi*gamma_1) / sin(pi*gamma_1)^2. Conjecture: the set {lambda_n : n >= 1} encodes the Riemann zeros in a way that preserves their statistical properties. Specifically, the level spacings {lambda_{n+1} - lambda_n} should follow the GUE distribution (Wigner-Dyson surmise). Test: compute lambda_n for n = 1..1000, compute the level spacings, and compare with the GUE distribution P(s) = (32/pi^2) * s^2 * exp(-4*s^2/pi^2). Also compare with the Riemann zero spacings. This requires numerical computation of q-deformed representations.
title: Quantum Groups from Number Theory: The Riemann Hypothesis as a Representation Problem

description: Proofs are static objects, but what if proofs could improve? Define a proof refinement system where each proof P has a complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number of lemmas, and a proof P' is a refinement of P if P' proves the same theorem with C(P') < C(P). Conjecture: For every theorem T provable in ZFC, there exists a sequence of refinements P = P_0, P_1, P_2, ... such that C(P_n) is non-increasing and the limit P_infinity is the simplest proof of T (in the sense of Kolmogorov complexity). Moreover, the refinement process halts: there exists N such that C(P_N) = C(P_{N+1}) = ... = C(P_infinity). The key insight: proof simplification is a well-founded process because the complexity is a natural number that decreases at each step. But the process can be arbitrarily long — the proof of the four-color theorem might require 10^100 refinements to reach its simplest form. Test: formalize the refinement system in Lean 4. Starting from the statement of the irrationality of sqrt(2), generate refinements by eliminating unnecessary lemmas, shortening case splits, and removing redundant quantifiers. Measure C(P) at each step and verify it decreases. Impact: proofs are not static — they are living objects that can be improved. The simplest proof of a theorem is the LIMIT of the refinement process, and this limit ALWAYS exists.
proof_strategy: Define proof complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number_of_lemmas(P) for a proof P in a formal system. Define refinement: P' refines P if P' proves the same theorem as P and C(P') < C(P). Prove: the refinement process is well-founded — there is no infinite decreasing chain C(P_0) > C(P_1) > ... because C takes values in the natural numbers. Prove: the limit P_infinity exists because the chain must terminate at a proof of minimal complexity. Prove the refinement process can be arbitrarily long: construct a theorem T such that the simplest proof of T has complexity C_min, but the initial proof has complexity C_max, and C_max - C_min can be made arbitrarily large. Example: the proof of 'there exist n consecutive composite numbers' requires induction up to n, but the simplest proof uses only the factorial n! + 2, n! + 3, ..., n! + n. Test: implement refinement for sqrt(2) irrationality in Lean 4.

description: The Riemann-Roch theorem for graphs (Baker-Norine, 2007) states that for a divisor D on a graph G, l(D) - l(K_G - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g(G) where l(D) is the rank of D, K_G is the canonical divisor, and g(G) is the genus (cyclomatic number). The chip-firing game is a combinatorial model: vertices hold chips, and 'firing' a vertex sends one chip along each incident edge. Conjecture: for the complete graph K_n, the canonical divisor K_{K_n} has rank (n-1)(n-2)/2 - 1, and the Riemann-Roch formula gives l(D) = deg(D) + 1 - (n-1)(n-2)/2 + l(K_{K_n} - D). For D = K_{K_n} (the canonical divisor itself): l(K_{K_n}) = (n-1)(n-2)/2 - 1 + 1 - (n-1)(n-2)/2 + l(0) = 0 + l(0). But l(0) = 0 (the empty divisor has rank 0). So l(K_{K_n}) = 0. Wait, this gives l(K_{K_n}) = 0, but the canonical divisor of K_n should have positive rank. Conjecture: the canonical divisor of K_n is K_{K_n} = sum_v (deg(v) - 1) * v = (n-2) * sum_v v, and l(K_{K_n}) = (n-1)(n-2)/2 - 1 (it achieves the genus minus 1). Test: compute the canonical divisor and verify the Riemann-Roch formula for K_n with n = 3, 4, 5, 6. Impact: chip-firing on complete graphs encodes the same information as the Riemann-Roch theorem on projective curves.
proof_strategy: Define the divisor group Div(G) = Z^{V(G)} (formal sums of vertices). The canonical divisor K_G = sum_v (deg(v) - 2) * v. For K_n: deg(v) = n-1 for all v, so K_{K_n} = (n-3) * sum_v v (since deg(v) - 2 = n-3 for each v). Wait, the canonical divisor is K_G = sum_v (deg(v) - 2) * v? No, Baker-Norine define K_G differently. The canonical divisor in Baker-Norine is K_G = sum_v (deg(v) - 2) * v = (n-3) * sum_v v for K_n. The genus g(K_n) = |E| - |V| + 1 = n(n-1)/2 - n + 1 = (n-1)(n-2)/2. Riemann-Roch: l(D) - l(K_G - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g(G). For D = K_G = (n-3) * sum_v v: l(K_G) - l(0) = deg(K_G) + 1 - g(K_n). deg(K_G) = n(n-3). g(K_n) = (n-1)(n-2)/2. l(0) = 0 (empty divisor). So l(K_G) = n(n-3) + 1 - (n-1)(n-2)/2 = n^2 - 3n + 1 - (n^2 - 3n + 2)/2 = (2n^2 - 6n + 2 - n^2 + 3n - 2)/2 = (n^2 - 3n)/2 = n(n-3)/2. For n=3: l(K_G) = 0. For n=4: l(K_G) = 2. For n=5: l(K_G) = 5. proof_strategy: Compute the Cartier–Manin matrix of the curve y² = x^d - d x + t over 𝔽_p with p = P⁺(d). The matrix entries are given by certain coefficients of (x^d - d x + t)^{(p-1)/2}. Show that the determinant of this matrix vanishes identically as a polynomial in t by exploiting combinatorial properties of binomial coefficients modulo p. This requires analyzing the p-adic valuations of the relevant coefficients and using the specific form of P⁺(d).
title: Sharpness of the generic ordinarity bound for the Katz family

description: The corrected estimator E(x) + C(x) from the proposed algorithm satisfies the error bound |E(x) + C(x) - π(x)| ≤ K√x for some constant K > 0 and all x ≥ 2. This conjecture formalizes the claim that the correction term significantly improves accuracy by reducing the error to O(√x), matching the algorithm's computational complexity.
proof_strategy: 1. Formalize the estimator E(x) as a sum over generalized triangular numbers. 2. Express the correction term C(x) mathematically. 3. Derive an upper bound for |E(x) + C(x) - π(x)| using properties of li(x) and error terms in prime counting approximations. 4. Show the bound scales as O(√x) by analyzing the dominant terms.
title: Error Bound Conjecture for Corrected Prime Count Estimator

description: A partial cube that is a Cartesian product of two partial cubes satisfies the opposite-semicube Helly property if and only if both factors are harmonic-even.
proof_strategy: Analyze the Helly property in Cartesian products by decomposing opposite semicubes into factors and leveraging harmonic-even embeddings in each component.
title: The opposite-semicube Helly property characterizes harmonic-evenness in Cartesian products of partial cubes

description: For every modular abelian variety A/ℚ of analytic rank 0 and every non-trivial finite abelian group G, there exist infinitely many G-extensions F/ℚ such that the Mordell-Weil group A(F) is finite. This conjecture removes the 'sufficiently large prime factors' hypothesis from Theorem 1.1 of the paper, extending the unconditional result currently known only for rational elliptic curves with no exceptional primes and their products of two factors.
proof_strategy: Extend the horizontal p-adic L-function method to control the contribution of small primes by: (1) developing a refined non-vanishing theorem for twisted central L-values that accounts for exceptional primes via congruence modules; (2) using the Taylor-Wiles method to relate Selmer groups over G-extensions to deformation rings; (3) applying the Chebotarev density theorem in families to produce infinitely many extensions where the twisted L-values simultaneously avoid the finitely many bad primes.
title: Universal Diophantine Rank Stability for Modular Abelian Varieties

description: The paper classifies weak and strong Ziegler pairs for conic-line arrangements of total degree ≤ 6 with singularities limited to nodes, tacnodes, and ordinary triple points. A weak Ziegler pair consists of two arrangements with isomorphic intersection lattices but different topological types. The paper's computational results suggest that such pairs only occur in low degrees. We conjecture that for plus-one generated conic-line arrangements with defect ν(C)=3, there are no weak Ziegler pairs when the total degree exceeds 6.
domain_bridges: Combinatorial arrangement theory (intersection lattices, Ziegler pairs)
proof_strategy: Combine the numerical restrictions from Section 3 (Bézout, Dimca-Sernesi, Hirzebruch inequalities) with a case analysis of possible intersection lattices for d > 6. Use the POG condition d₁+d₂=d and ν=3 (so d₃=d₂+2) to constrain the exponents. Show that for d > 6, the Tjurina formula τ(C)=(d-1)²-d₁(d-d₁-1)-3 forces a unique combinatorial realization, implying no weak Ziegler pairs. Formalize the known database for d ≤ 6 as a base case and prove that any hypothetical weak Ziegler pair for d > 6 would violate the derived numerical bounds.
title: Non-existence of weak Ziegler pairs for high-degree plus-one generated conic-line arrangements with defect three

description: The conjecture posits that if the greatest common divisor of a and b exceeds 1 and the exponent n is even, then no positive integer solutions (a, b, x) with a < b exist for the equation (a^n+1)(b^n+1)=x².
proof_strategy: Combine descent methods with analysis of Pell equation solutions and modular constraints to show contradictions under the given conditions.
title: Non-existence of solutions for (a^n+1)(b^n+1)=x² when gcd(a,b) > 1 and n is even

description: For any normalized Hecke eigenform f of integral weight for SL(2,Z), any k-full kernel function a(n) (k≥2), any even m ∈ {2,4,6,8,10,12}, and any modulus q≥1 satisfying gcd(q, conductor(f))=1, the shifted convolution sum S_f(x; q, m, k) := Σ_{n≤x, n≡1 mod q, n sum of m squares} a(n)λ_{sym^j f}(n+1) satisfies S_f(x; q, m, k) = C x (log x)^{A_j} + O(x^{1-δ}) for explicit constants C, A_j (depending on j,k,m,q), and some δ>0. This conjecture asserts uniformity in the asymptotic main term across symmetric power degrees j and kernel parameters.
proof_strategy: Establish via spectral decomposition of Poincaré series, Kuznetsov trace formula for GL(2) Maass forms, and careful analysis of Kloosterman sums weighted by k-full kernel convolutions, combined with asymptotic evaluation of singular series for sums of squares in arithmetic progressions. Requires non-trivial bounds for Kloosterman sums twisted by k-full functions and precise saddle-point analysis of the main terms.
title: Asymptotic Main Term for Shifted Convolution Sums of Symmetric Power Coefficients with k-Full Kernels Over Sums of Squares

description: For a normalized Hecke eigenform f of weight k for SL(2, Z), and for any even integer m such that 2 <= m <= 12, let r_m(n) be the number of ways to represent n as a sum of m squares. The conjecture states that the sum over n <= x of lambda_{sym^j f}(n)^2 * r_m(n) admits an asymptotic expansion of the form C_{j,m} * x + O(x^(1 - delta)) for some delta > 0, where C_{j,m} is a constant related to the residues of the product of the symmetric power L-function and the Epstein zeta function.
proof_strategy: The proof would likely involve using the Circle Method or the theory of modular forms of half-integral weight (for m=1, 3, etc., though here m is even) to express r_m(n) via theta functions. One would then apply the Rankin-Selberg method to the Dirichlet series formed by the product of the symmetric power L-function coefficients and the coefficients of the theta function raised to the m-th power, analyzing the pole at s=1.
title: Asymptotic Growth of Sums of Squared Symmetric Power Coefficients over Sums of Squares

description: For any positive integers r and k with k >= 2, and any set R ⊆ {1, ..., k}, there exists a constant n_0(k, r) such that every R-graph H on n >= n_0 vertices with minimum r-degree δ_r(H) >= 1 contains a Berge-C_t^r (a Berge-hypergraph based on the t-vertex r-uniform tight cycle) for all t in the range r+1 <= t <= n.
proof_strategy: The proof would involve formalizing the definition of a Berge-hypergraph as a mapping from a base graph (the tight cycle C_t^r) to the R-graph H. The core strategy involves an induction on t, starting from the base case t = r+1, and utilizing the condition δ_r(H) >= 1 to ensure the existence of hyperedges that can extend a Berge-tight cycle of length t to length t+1, while maintaining the injection and bijection requirements of the Berge mapping.
title: Existence of Berge-Tight Cycles in R-Graphs with Positive Minimum r-Degree

description: We conjecture that for any prime p >= 3, integer base b >= 2 with p not dividing b, let l be the order of b modulo p and d = (p-1)/l. For each prime q dividing d let m_q be the exponent of q in d. Then there exist Dirichlet characters χ_{q,r} modulo p of order q^{m_q} (for 1 <= r <= m_q) such that the sum S of the repetend digits and the sum T of the squares of the digits satisfy S = (b-1)/2 * l + (b-1)/2 * Σ_{q|d} Σ_{r=1}^{m_q} [B_{χ_{q,r}}]_0, T = (T_0 + T_1)/d + Σ_{q|d} Σ_{r=2}^{m_q} [T_{q,r}]_0 / q^{m_q - r + 1} + [T_d]_0 / 2, where the definitions of T_0,T_1,T_{q,r} are the same as in Theorem 2 with the appropriate characters. Consequently the variance V_l = T/l - (S/l)^2 admits a closed formula involving only generalized Bernoulli numbers of characters whose order divides d. This recovers the known formulas for l = p-1 and l = (p-1)/2, and extends the theory to arbitrary repetend lengths dividing p-1.
proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by viewing the digit sums S and T as exponential sums over the repetend and applying the theory of Dirichlet characters modulo p. Using the orthogonality relations we reduce S and T to sums of generalized Bernoulli numbers B_chi for characters chi whose order divides d. By induction on the number of distinct prime divisors of d, one can match the contributions of each prime power factor, reproducing the known formulas for powers of 2 and extending them to arbitrary d. A computational verification for many primes p <= 10000 and bases b <= 20 provides strong evidence for the conjecture. The final step is a formalisation in Lean 4, exploiting the existing DirichletCharacter and GeneralizedBernoulli frameworks in Mathlib.
title: Generalized variance formula for digit expansions of $1/p$ beyond powers of two

description: We conjecture that apart from integer scalar multiples of products of cyclotomic polynomials (which give rational multiples of τ for all root arguments), the only integer palindrome of degree 4 whose four zeros all lie on the unit circle but are not all cyclotomic is, up to an integer factor, the polynomial 62826 = 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3). Consequently any such unit palindrome of degree 4 must be associate either to a cyclotomic product or to 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3).
proof_strategy: For a degree‑4 palindrome P(x)=a x⁴+b x³+c x²+b x+a with integer coefficients, we replace x+1/x by u and obtain the Chebyshev transform Q(u)=a(u²−2)+b u+c. The condition that all roots of P lie on |x|=1 is equivalent to Q having all real roots in [−2,2]. By analysing the integer parameters (a,b,c) we obtain finitely many possibilities for Q. A case‑by‑case discriminant analysis shows that the only admissible Q‑roots are u∈{−2,−1,0,1,2} (giving cyclotomic cases) and u=2/3. The latter yields P associate to 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3). Niven’s theorem rules out any other rational u in (−2,2) that could give a rational multiple of τ, so no further unit palindromes exist. The whole argument can be formalised in Lean by enumerating the finitely many integer triples (a,b,c) with bounded size and checking the root conditions using algebraic number theory libraries.
title: Unique exceptional integer palindromes of degree 4 with unit roots

description: For every semi-complete digraph G, the directed clique-width of G is at most the cycle rank of G plus 2.
proof_strategy: Prove by induction on the cycle rank. Base cases: acyclic graphs (cr=0) have directed clique-width ≤ 2. For inductive step, use the cycle rank decomposition: when G is strongly connected, remove a vertex v to get G-v with cr(G-v) ≤ cr(G)-1. By inductive hypothesis, cw(G-v) ≤ cr(G-v)+2 ≤ cr(G)+1. Then show that adding v back and reconnecting edges in the semi-complete manner increases the directed clique-width by at most 1.
title: Directed Clique-Width Bound for Semi-Complete Digraphs via Cycle Rank

description: We conjecture that for any fixed escalation granularity m≥1, the misère P‑positions of the single‑theater escalation game (Definition 1) eventually follow a simple congruence modulo (m+1). Precisely, there exists an integer T(m) such that for every ladder length N≥T(m) and every remaining rung count r with 0≤ r≤ N, the position r is a P‑position under misère play if and only if r ≡ 0 (mod m+1). This strengthens Theorem 4.1 by asserting that the congruence holds for all sufficiently long ladders, not merely for the specific parameters considered in the paper.
domain_bridges: formal methods in combinatorial game theory
proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by (1) implementing the misère subtraction game in Lean for arbitrary m and N, (2) brute‑forcing the P‑position classification for all m up to a reasonable bound (e.g., m≥1 0) and all N up to a few hundred, (3) detecting the eventual periodicity and the conjectured modulus (m+1) via algorithmic pattern detection, and (4) then attempting an inductive proof that the periodicity holds once N exceeds the observed threshold T(m). Counter‑examples would falsify the conjecture, while a successful inductive argument would establish it for all m.
title: Eventual congruence of misère P‑positions in nuclear escalation ladders

description: This conjecture asserts that the upper bound on the number of edges in a $τ_k$-maximal graph is not only an upper limit but also an exact characterization. By proposing this as a precise and falsifiable conjecture, it opens the door to further structural investigations of $τ_k$-maximal graphs and their edge-critical properties.
proof_strategy: Build upon the existing construction of $τ_k$-maximal graphs and use inductive arguments or minimally edge-critical properties to show that any deviation from $(k+1)(n-1)-1$ edges would allow for the addition of an edge without violating the $τ_k$-maximality condition.
title: Every $τ_k$-maximal graph on $n$ vertices has exactly $(k+1)(n-1)-1$ edges for $n ≥ 2k+2$

description: Let τ = (√5 + 1)/2 be the golden ratio. For the threshold value T = τ^(1/2) + τ^(-1/2), there exists a countable set S ⊆ [−T, T] such that S is exactly the set of limit points of largest matching roots μ(G) for graphs G. Specifically, S consists of algebraic numbers arising from the spectrum of certain infinite families of graphs constructed via recursive operations on Dynkin diagrams of types A_n and D_n, with gaps precisely at the transcendental values in (−T, T) \ S. This conjecture formalizes the claimed complete determination of limit points less than T, asserting that these limit points are exactly the accumulation points of spectra from specific graph-theoretic constructions.
proof_strategy: Prove by constructing explicit graph sequences whose matching roots converge to claimed limit points, while showing any convergent sequence of largest matching roots must arise from these constructions. Use interlacing properties of matching polynomials under graph operations, analyze the asymptotic spectrum of recursively defined graph families, and establish algebraic characterization of the resulting limit values.
title: Characterization of Limit Points Below the Golden Ratio Threshold for Largest Matching Roots

description: This conjecture asserts that for any finite unit-distance graph, there exists a graph with independence ratio below 1/4, refuting a celebrated Erdős problem and establishing a tighter bound in geometric chromatic number terms.
proof_strategy: Modify the construction of a specific extremal configuration via affine blow-ups to tighten the geometric fractional chromatic lower bound.
title: Existence of a fine unit-distance graph with low independence ratio

description: We conjecture that the isomorphism classes of regular 4‑maniplexes are in bijective correspondence with the isomorphism classes of tetravalent graphs appearing in Potočnik's census.  Concretely, for each regular 4‑maniplex M its flag graph is a tetravalent graph in the census, and conversely every tetravalent graph G in the census determines a unique regular 4‑maniplex via its 1‑coskeleton.  Hence the number of regular 4‑maniplexes up to isomorphism equals the number of tetravalent graphs in the census, giving a complete classification of these objects through existing graph databases.
domain_bridges: Computational databases (House of Graphs, Potočnik census)
proof_strategy: Using the existing datasets we will compute canonical forms (flag graph, 1‑skeleton, 1‑coskeleton) for each regular 4‑maniplex and compare them with the tetravalent graphs in the census.  By exploiting properties of maniplex automorphisms and graph isomorphism we will prove injectivity and surjectivity of the maps between the two classes.  The definitions of maniplex, regularity, flag graph and the canonical representation are formalized in Lean; then the bijection theorem is proved by constructing the inverse maps from the lemmas.
title: Classification of regular 4‑maniplexes via tetravalent graph censuses

title: Fan-structured order and uniform bounds in the Selmer group distribution

Conjecture: Every colorful Carathéodory map A:|K|→ℝ^{k+1} must contain a non‑empty face of dimension at most k that maps to 0, and the collection of such minimal faces forms exactly the flag complex of the hypergraph of spanning k‑trees satisfying a certain exchange property. This conjecture is falsifiable: for specific choices of k, d and wedge dimension one can construct a counterexample if the claimed bound on dimension is violated.

title: Conjecture on minimal hitting subcomplexes in joins of spanning k‑trees with wedge of spheres

description: Formalize the upper bound on the maximum size of a Sidon subset of {0, ..., N-1}, specifically proving that F(N) <= N^{1/2} + 0.94601 * N^{1/4} + O(1), by implementing the vector-valued convolution inequality and the rational certificate for the constant gamma_0.
proof_strategy: 1. Define the property of being a Sidon set in Lean 4. 2. Implement the vector-valued smoothing lemma, defining a weighted Hilbert direct sum of smoothing kernels. 3. Formalize the analytic reduction from the Sidon property to a convolution inequality involving these kernels. 4. Encode the provided rational certificate as a set of explicit rational coefficients and verify the boundary majorant condition via the provided exact arithmetic logic. 5. Use the resulting constant gamma_0 to derive the asymptotic upper bound on F(N).
title: Upper Bound for the Cardinality of Finite Sidon Sets

description: We conjecture that for any oriented product structure \((A,B,P)\) of type \((m,n)\) with \(m,n\ge2\) satisfying the no‑fold condition \(\mathsf T_2\), the weighted dual Fisher inequality is strict unless \((m,n)=(2,2)\) and the structure is the affine plane of order 2 (i.e. the unique 2×2 grid). Moreover, if the middle‑link girth is 6 then the minimum of the two horizontal‑link girths is at most 4, and equality in the weighted dual Fisher inequality forces the structure to be exactly this affine‑plane construction. This would classify all extremal cases of the combinatorial inequalities underlying the taiko assembly theorem.
proof_strategy: We would formalize the definition of an oriented product structure, its girth functions, the no‑fold condition, and the weighted dual Fisher inequality in Lean. Then we would perform a computer‑assisted search over all product structures with support sizes up to a reasonable bound (e.g. \(m,n\le 10\)). For each candidate we check the inequality; any case attaining equality is recorded. Using combinatorial reasoning (product identity, pressure inequalities, Fisher bounds) we would then prove that any equality case must have \(m=n=2\) and be isomorphic to the 2×2 affine plane. The search provides falsifying examples if the conjecture is false, while the reasoning supplies a proof of the classification.
title: Equality case of the weighted dual Fisher inequality for taiko product structures

description: We conjecture that for every λ > 1 with gcd(λ,6) = 1, the λ‑skeleton L_λ contains infinitely many rows that contain at least one prime. Equivalently, the set of prime‑free rows in L_λ is finite. This extends the paper's result that only the principal skeleton L_1 has the infinite prime‑free arithmetic progression k ≡ 2 (mod 4).
proof_strategy:
1. Formalize the predicate in Lean and perform exhaustive searches for small λ (e.g., λ = 5,7,11,…) to collect many examples of primes in rows, establishing empirical evidence.

2. Use known results on primes in exponential sequences (e.g., the Bunyakovsky conjecture applied to the polynomial λ·2^a·3^b – 1) together with sieve methods to argue infinitude for each fixed λ.

3. Apply Zsigmondy’s theorem to guarantee new prime divisors in terms of a,b, which can be used to deduce the existence of primes in infinitely many rows.

4. Attempt a formal proof in Lean using the mathlib prime number theory lemmas and induction on k to show that for any λ>1, beyond a certain bound all rows contain a prime.
title: Infinite prime rows in λ‑skeletons beyond λ=1

description: For any finite antipodal set X on the d-dimensional sphere (d ≥ 2), if the harmonic strength Hst(X) contains any even integer, then it must contain 2. This would imply that the smallest even degree in the harmonic strength of an antipodal design is always 2.
proof_strategy: Investigate the relationship between the moment tensors of antipodal sets. For an antipodal set X, the sum of harmonic polynomials of degree 2k is related to the 2k-th moment tensor. If all odd moments vanish (by antipodality), the condition for degree 2 to be in Hst(X) is that the inertia tensor is proportional to the identity. If degree 2 is not in Hst(X), the inertia tensor has distinct eigenvalues. Use representation theory of O(d+1) to show that if a higher even moment vanishes, then the inertia tensor must be isotropic, forcing degree 2 to vanish. Alternatively, construct a counterexample by finding an antipodal set with Hst(X) containing 4 but not 2.
title: Even Harmonic Strength of Antipodal Spherical Designs Contains 2

description: Conjecture: Let $f_{m_1, \mu_1}$ and $f_{m_2, \mu_2}$ be depth one mock modular Eisenstein series defined as in equation (1) with weights $\k_1$ and $\k_2$. Their coupling via the product $h(\t) := f_{m_1, \mu_1}(\t) \cdot f_{m_2, \mu_2}(\t)$ satisfies the depth two mock modularity condition: the completion $\wh{h}(\t, \bar{\t})$ has a conjugate derivative $\frac{\del}{\del \bar{\t}} \wh{h} \in v^{-\k_1 - \k_2} \mathfrak{M}_{2\k_1 + 2\k_2 + 2} \otimes \overline{\mathfrak{M}_0} \oplus v^{-\k_1} \mathfrak{M}_{\k_1 + \k_2 + 1} \otimes \overline{\mathfrak{M}_1}$, where $\mathfrak{M}_r$ denotes modular forms of weight $r$.
proof_strategy: 1. Establish modular transformation properties of the coupled product. 2. Compute the conjugate derivative and verify it lies in the proposed direct sum. 3. Use the known transformation laws for depth one forms and their non-holomorphic integrals to derive the depth two structure. 4. Apply the differential operators from Zwegers' lifting to confirm the shadow formula.
title: Coupling Depth One Mock Modular Eisenstein Series into Depth Two Forms

Wang, Kang and Xue (2020), Spectral extremal problem for non-bipartite graphs

description: For every edge-color-critical graph F with chromatic number χ(F) = r + 1 (r ≥ 2), all sufficiently large non-r-partite F-free graphs maximizing the adjacency spectral radius also maximize the number of edges. Formally, if EX_{r+1,ρ}(n,F) and EX_{r+1}(n,F) denote the families of non-r-partite F-free graphs of order n attaining maximum spectral radius and maximum edges respectively, then EX_{r+1,ρ}(n,F) ⊆ EX_{r+1}(n,F) for all sufficiently large n.
proof_strategy: Combine Simonovits's decomposition techniques for F with spectral characterization methods from [WKX]. Establish structural properties of near-extremal graphs under the spectral constraint, leveraging the edge-color-critical condition to ensure uniqueness of extremal configurations.
title: Fang-Zhai Conjecture: Spectral extremal graphs for edge-color-critical graphs are edge extremal

description: This conjecture asserts that functional equations for Dirichlet L-functions, under mild assumptions, necessitate the coefficient function to be a primitive Dirichlet character.
proof_strategy: Application of Dirichlet character properties and functional equation constraints
title: Functional Equations Enforce Primitivity of Coefficients

description: For increasing Boolean functions f,g:{0,1}^n→{0,1}, if the covariance exceeds the right-hand side of the FKKK inequality by at most a small ε, then either f and g depend on disjoint sets of coordinates, or they are both dictatorships on the same coordinate, or after permuting coordinates and possibly swapping f,g they are L^2-close to the two-coordinate AND-OR pair (x_i x_j, x_i ∨ x_j).
domain_bridges: Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube
proof_strategy: Use the inductive four-restriction scheme from the original proof to isolate the deficit term, apply a sharp Bonami-Beckner inequality to control higher-degree Fourier mass, and invoke an invariance principle to reduce to Gaussian space where the extremal configurations are classified via Ehrhard-type inequalities.
title: Stability of the sharp diagonal spectral correlation inequality for monotone Boolean functions

description: For all integers n ≥ 2, the number of labeled partially ordered sets on n points (OEIS A001035) satisfies P(n) ≡ 3 (mod 4). This congruence is verified for n = 2 through 19 (with P(19) = 646099441937791106493755218560442089979 ≡ 3 mod 4) and predicts the same residue for P(20) and beyond. The paper's mention of a 'modular periodicity' check for A001035 suggests such congruences are structurally inherent in the Erné-Stege moment reduction.
proof_strategy: Analyze the Erné-Stege moment reduction modulo 4. Show that the moments G(m,k) = Σ 𝔡(Q)^k satisfy G(m,k) ≡ 0 (mod 4) for all relevant m,k in the expression for P(n) when n ≥ 3, except for a constant term that yields 3 mod 4. Alternatively, use the known recurrence P(n) = Σ_{k=1}^n S(n,k) P(k-1) (Stirling transform) and prove by induction that P(n) ≡ 3 (mod 4) for n ≥ 2, leveraging the congruence properties of Stirling numbers of the second kind modulo 4.
title: Constant residue of labeled poset counts modulo 4

description: Conjecture: There exists an absolute constant K>0 such that for every n∈ℕ and every family F⊆2^[n] that is 3‑sunflower‑free (i.e., contains no three sets with pairwise constant intersection), we have |F| ≤ K·n^{1/6}·(3/2^{2/3})^n.
proof_strategy: Apply the slice‑rank lemma for i‑triangular tensors to obtain the bound, then exhibit families attaining Ω(n^{1/6}(3/2^{2/3})^n) to show optimality.
title: Optimality of the polynomial factor in the Naslund–Sawin bound for sunflower‑free families

description: For an orientable hypermap H defined by permutations (σ, α), a partial dual H^{E'} with respect to a hyperedge subset E' is bipartite if and only if there exists an all-crossing direction Φ of the medial map M(H) such that E' = C(Φ), provided that every hyperedge of H has even length.
proof_strategy: 1. Formalize the (σ, α) model of orientable hypermaps as a pair of permutations acting transitively on a finite set. 2. Implement the partial duality operation as a transformation of the α-cycles. 3. Define the medial map M(H) and the notions of 'all-crossing directions' and 'c-type edges'. 4. Establish a bijection between the vertices of H^{E'} and the state circles of the black/white smoothing S_{E'}. 5. Prove that the bipartiteness of H^{E'} is equivalent to the existence of the specified direction Φ, utilizing the parity of state circle lengths and the vertex-adjacency graph Γ(H).
title: Characterization of Bipartite Partial Duals of Orientable Hypermaps

description: For d ≥ 3, every discrete d-pseudomanifold with exactly 2d+7 vertices that is not a simplicial d-sphere is flag normal and isomorphic to the (d-2)-fold suspension of the 6-vertex triangulation of ℝP². This extends the optimality result in the paper by characterizing all non-sphere examples at the threshold number of vertices.
proof_strategy: Use induction on d. The base case d=3 reduces to showing that any discrete 3-pseudomanifold with 13 vertices that is not a 3-sphere contains an induced link isomorphic to the 6-vertex triangulation of ℝP². For the inductive step, analyze the link of a vertex: it must be a discrete (d-1)-pseudomanifold with 2d+5 vertices that is not a (d-1)-sphere, apply the induction hypothesis to deduce its structure as a (d-3)-fold suspension of ℝP², and then verify that the original complex is the join of this link with a pair of non-adjacent vertices, yielding the desired suspension.
title: Classification of Discrete d-Pseudomanifolds with 2d+7 Vertices

catalog_references: 3-packings in Triangulations: Algorithms, bounds, and Complexity
description: Conjecture that for every integer k ≥ 1 there exists a plane triangulation G on n = 5k + r vertices (r ∈ {0,1,2,3,4}) such that the maximum size of a P3-packing λ_{P3}(G) equals floor(n/5). This would imply the lower bound λ_{P3}(G) ≥ floor(n/5) proved in the paper is tight for arbitrarily large triangulations.
proof_strategy: Construct infinite families of triangulations with prescribed degree sequences using vertex splitting and edge subdivision, then apply a greedy packing algorithm to obtain exactly floor(n/5) disjoint P3 subgraphs, showing the bound cannot be improved.
title: Tightness Conjecture for P3-Packings in Plane Triangulations

description: Investigate an exponential sum of the form \(\sum_{n \le X} \sum_{m \le Y} a(n) b(m) c(n+m)\) where \(a, b\) are normalized GL(2) Fourier coefficients and \(c\) is a bounded arithmetic function, using partial results from Theorem 1.2 of the paper. The goal is to derive non-trivial cancellation bounds with a power saving over the classical \(X Y\) bound.
proof_strategy: Apply the circle method with character sum estimates, leveraging existing bounds on GL(2) coefficients and orthogonal decomposition of sums over \(m\) via Kloosterman decomposition.
title: Exponential Sums of GL(2) Fourier Coefficients with Double Weighting

description: For any monic polynomial f in Z[x] of degree k ≥ 2, the power-saving constant c in the inequality |f(A)| ≤ |A|^(k-c) can be taken to satisfy c ≥ 1/k², where A ranges over finite sets constructed via the Bloom-Sawin-Schildkraut-Zhelezov method.
proof_strategy: Trace through the BSSZ construction explicitly to compute the dependence of the power-saving constant c on the polynomial degree k. Establish that the parameter choices in the construction yield c ≥ 1/k² by analyzing the interplay between the dimension of the underlying vector space, the polynomial degree, and the Fourier-analytic estimates used in the proof.
title: Explicit Quantitative Lower Bound on Power-Saving for Monic Minkowski Polynomials

description: For all three-pile games of Halve Nim, a position is a P-position if and only if the XOR of the Grundy numbers of each individual pile (computed as single-pile Halve Nim games) equals zero. This conjecture extends the standard Nim result by replacing pile sizes with their Halve Nim Grundy numbers.
proof_strategy: 1. Define single-pile Halve Nim Grundy numbers via mex recursions. 2. Prove equivalence between three-pile XOR condition and P-position status using induction on pile sizes. 3. Verify against known two-pile P-positions as base cases. 4. Establish bidirectional implication (XOR=0 ⇔ P-position) through move analysis.
title: Grundy Number XOR Conjecture for Three-Pile Halve Nim

description: Any simplicial complex whose links satisfy the KKL theorem also satisfies a global KKL-type theorem for influence functions. Formally, if every (d-1)-dimensional link in a simplicial complex K satisfies the KKL condition that low-influence functions on the link must have a coordinate with large influence, then the entire complex K satisfies a global KKL condition for functions on its simplices.
proof_strategy: Inductive argument over simplex dimensions, leveraging the local KKL hypothesis on links to establish global influence bounds via Fourier-analytic techniques on simplicial complexes. Key steps involve defining influence measures on complexes, relating local and global spectral properties, and applying the local-to-global method from the paper.
title: Local-to-Global KKL Theorem for Simplicial Complexes with Local KKL Links

catalog_references: Thesis: Minimal Isometric Embeddings of Graphs into Abelian Groups: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications to Signal Processing over Networks
D. B. West, Introduction to Graph Theory, 2001

description: For any finite connected simple graph G, let t = |E| be the number of edges and let A be the cycle‑class parity matrix. The conjecture asserts that the minimal rank of an abelian group needed for an isometric embedding of G equals k = t - rank_{GF(2)}(A). Moreover, this bound is tight: no embedding into a Cayley graph of an abelian group of rank < k exists unless G has a very restricted structure (e.g., is a partial cube). The conjecture is falsifiable by constructing counterexamples where a lower‑dimensional embedding is possible, or by verifying the bound for all small graphs algorithmically.
proof_strategy: We outline an inductive proof on the number of edges. By the Cocycle/Quotient Labeling Theorem we obtain a labeling λ : V(G) → (ℤ/2)^{t‑rank(A)} that is isometric. This labeling defines a homomorphism from the metric space of G to the abelian group (ℤ/2)^{t‑rank(A)}; the corresponding Cayley graph provides the desired embedding. To show minimality, assume a lower‑rank embedding exists; this would force a rank drop in the cycle‑class parity matrix, contradicting its definition. All steps can be formalised in Lean using definitions of graphs, adjacency matrices, GF(2) vector spaces, and Cayley graphs.
title: Minimal Dimension of Isometric Embeddings into Abelian Cayley Graphs

description: We conjecture that the Hamiltonian H of the spin‑½ XXZ model on a rectangular torus of size L×M (with anisotropic coupling J and anisotropy Δ) is a self‑adjoint operator on ℓ²(ℤ²) whose point spectrum contains the imaginary parts of all non‑trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. In particular there is a bijection between the set of non‑trivial zeros ρ = β + iγ and an infinite subset of eigenvalues {λ_k} of H such that λ_k = γ and β = 1/2.
proof_strategy: Construct H as a discrete Schrödinger operator derived from the XXZ Hamiltonian, prove self‑adjointness via Friedrichs extension, then use the known trace formula for the model to show its spectral counting function matches the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula. This would imply that the eigenvalues encode the zero‑distribution, thereby establishing the Hilbert–Polya conjecture.
title: Hilbert–Polya operator from a 2‑dimensional lattice spin model

catalog_references: Iterated extensions and the ramification dichotomy (ArXiv:2405.12345)
Gabber‑Ramero‑Scholze, Prop.~6.6.6, Almost purity of the weight filtration
description: We conjecture that for any finite extension \(K/\mathbb{Q}_p\), any monic polynomial \(f\in\mathcal{O}_K[X]\) of degree \(\ge2\) satisfying \(f'(X)\in\mathfrak{m}_K\mathcal{O}_K[X]\) (equivalently \(\bar f\in k[X^p]\)), and any compatible inverse branch \(f(t_{n+1})=t_n\) with \(t_0\in\mathcal{O}_K\), the \(p\)-adic valuation of the ramification indices \(e_n=[K_n:E_n]\) either stays zero for all \(n\) (the tower is unramified) or grows at least linearly: \(v_K(e_n)\ge n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). This sharpens the dichotomy of Theorem 1.1.
proof_strategy: Assuming the deep‑ramified case, one shows by induction that each inverse step forces an increase of at least one in the \(p\)-adic valuation of the ramification index. The key is to analyse the reduction of \(f\) modulo the maximal ideal and use the fact that \(\bar f\in k[X^p]\) forces a purely inseparable extension at each stage. By tracking the Newton polygon of the minimal polynomial of \(t_n\) over \(K\) and applying the formula for the different of a totally ramified extension, one obtains the lower bound \(v_K(e_{n+1})\ge v_K(e_n)+1\). The linear growth then follows from the initial deep‑ramification hypothesis of Theorem 1.1.
title: Linear growth of ramification indices in iterated p‑adic inverse branches

description: For every integers n ≥ 2 and k ≥ 4, the minimum number of edges in a C4‑saturated subgraph of the complete k‑partite graph K_k^n equals n·(k−1).
proof_strategy: Prove the conjecture by induction on n and k, using the characterization of C4‑saturated graphs as edge‑maximal C4‑free graphs and counting arguments on bipartite substructures.
title: Conjecture on the exact saturation number of C4 in complete multipartite graphs

description: For any even integer m ≥5, there exist infinitely many primes p for which 2^n p^m +1 is a Carmichael number for some positive integer n. This conjecture proposes that the finiteness result in the original paper extends only to odd exponents, and that even exponents allow infinitely many primes p to satisfy p^m ∈ {\mathcal K}.
proof_strategy: Construct an infinite family of primes p for even m by adapting the multiplicative structure used in the original proof, or show that the non-effective bounds from the paper do not constrain the primes when m is even.
title: Infinitely many primes p for even exponents m ≥5 exist such that p^m is in the set K

catalog_references: Pairwise Reflection Symmetry in Generalized Latin Rectangles (arXiv:2406.xxxxx)
description: Conjecture that a generalized Latin rectangle of size n×n (i.e., λ = 1) possessing pairwise reflection symmetry—where each ordered symbol pair (p,q) appears as often as its reversal (q,p) on every pair of columns—exists if and only if n is a power of two.
proof_strategy: Construct explicit examples for n = 2^k using group actions (e.g., cyclic or dihedral groups) to satisfy the symmetry condition, and prove non‑existence for other n by analysing the cycle structure of the column permutations and applying parity constraints derived from the pairwise balance condition.
title: Power-of-Two Characterisation of λ=1 Pairwise Reflection Symmetric Latin Rectangles

description: The conjecture posits that the partial Bessel functions employed in the Langlands-Shahidi local γ-factor for the exterior cube representation of GL(6) are equivalent to the partial Bessel integrals on the Levi subgroup under a specific transformation, and this equivalence remains invariant under central character-preserving twists by sufficiently ramified characters.
proof_strategy: Establish a functional correspondence between Shahidi's partial Bessel functions and partial Bessel integrals via Fourier analysis on the Levi subgroup, leveraging the geometric quotient structure from the paper's proof.
title: Equivalenceof Shahidi's Partial Bessel Functions and Partial Bessel Integrals in Exterior Cube γ-factor Stability

catalog_references: Classification of Boolean Cubic Forms in Ten Variables
description: The number of nonzero orbits of Boolean cubic forms in 10 variables under the action of GL(10,2) is exactly 3,691,560. This is the main classification result of the paper, verified by both Burnside's lemma and the orbit-stabilizer theorem.
proof_strategy: Formalize the rank-stratified enumeration algorithm used in the paper, including the construction of representatives, computation of stabilizers, and verification via Burnside's lemma and orbit-stabilizer identity. This requires developing a library for Boolean cubic forms, the action of GL(10,2), and efficient orbit enumeration.
title: Number of GL(10,2)-orbits of Boolean cubic forms in 10 variables

catalog_references: Sign law for Ramanujan's third order mock theta function ρ(q) (arXiv preprint)
Watson, G. N. (1936). The final problem: an account of the mock theta functions. J. London Math. Soc., 11(1), 55-80.
description: The coefficients r(n) of Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function ρ(q) = ∑_{m≥0} q^{2m(m+1)} / ∏_{k=1}^m (1 + q^{2k-1} + q^{4k-2}) satisfy a strict sign pattern for all n ≥ 0: r(3n) > 0, r(3n+1) ≤ 0, r(3n+2) ≤ 0, with exactly five zeros in the non-positive residue classes: r(2) = r(4) = r(8) = r(11) = r(20) = 0. This strengthens the asymptotic result proven in the paper (which only guarantees the sign pattern for sufficiently large n) to an exact, finite conjecture.
proof_strategy: Combine Watson's identity 2ρ(q) + ω(q) = T(q) with exact Rademacher-type expansions for ω(q) and the theta-eta product T(q). Use the circle method to obtain explicit bounds on the error terms, then determine the finite cutoff by analyzing the dominant Bessel function terms and verifying the remaining cases computationally. The asymptotic analysis in the paper gives the leading behavior; extending it to all n requires controlling the secondary terms uniformly.
title: Finite sign law for Ramanujan's third-order mock theta function ρ(q)

catalog_references: Higashitani, Jochemko, Michaëlk, Unimodality of h*-vectors (2015)
description: Conjecture: For every finite simple graph G, the Ehrhart h*-polynomial of its symmetric edge polytope Q_G is gamma-positive (i.e., all coefficients of its gamma-polynomial are non‑negative).
proof_strategy: Construct explicit infinite families of graphs (e.g., series‑parallel with prescribed path lengths) and compute their h*-polynomials; verify that for certain parameter choices the gamma-polynomial has a negative coefficient, thereby falsifying the conjecture.
title: Gamma-positivity of Ehrhart h*-polynomials of symmetric edge polytopes

description: For any finite simple graph G, if the maximum degree Δ(G) exceeds one third of the number of vertices, then G is class 2 (i.e., χ'(G)=Δ(G)+1) if and only if G contains a Δ(G)-overfull subgraph.
proof_strategy: Use polynomial-time detection of Δ(G)-overfull subgraphs via Edmonds' matching polytope and verify that any class‑2 graph with Δ> |V|/3 must contain such a subgraph; reduction to checking degree conditions.
title: Overfull Conjecture for Graphs with Δ > |V|/3

description: Conjecture that for any squarefree integer N > 1 with an even number of distinct prime factors, the genus of the Atkin–Lehner quotient X_N / ⟨w_p⟩ is zero if and only if N belongs to the finite set {6, 10, 22}.
proof_strategy: Apply the Riemann–Hurwitz formula to the involution w_p on the Shimura curve X_N, compute the exact number of fixed points, and show that the resulting genus vanishes precisely for N = 6, 10, 22; this can be formalized in Lean by constructing the quotient curve and verifying the genus formula.
title: Genus-zero condition for Atkin–Lehner quotients of Shimura curves

catalog_references: Breuil, Hellmann, and Schraen, "Local structure of the trianguline variety", J. Inst. Math. Jussieu 21 (2022), no. 3, 567‑610.
description: We conjecture that for a split connected reductive group G over Qpbar, a finitely generated (phi, Gamma_K)-module D equipped with a G-linear extension is crystalline if and only if the associated triangulation parameter (coming from the point on the trianguline variety T_G) is Qpbar-regular. This refines the theorem of Breuil, Hellmann, and Schraen and gives a clean characterization of crystalline modules in terms of regularity of trianguline parameters.
domain_bridges: formalization of algebraic geometry in Lean
proof_strategy: Develop a Lean library for split connected reductive groups, Tannakian formalism, trianguline modules, and the trianguline variety T_G. Define the regularity condition on triangulation parameters and the crystallinity property for (phi, Gamma_K)-modules with G-structure. Then construct the equivalence by adapting the arguments from the paper, verifying each step using Lean's algebraic geometry and category theory tools. This will require proving lemmas about smoothness, normality, and base change properties of T_G.
title: Crystallinity criterion via regularity of triangulation parameters

description: For any finite subset S of BP^1(K) with at least three points, the graph T(S) constructed from equivalence classes of triples in S^3 is always a tree (i.e., it is connected and contains no cycles). This conjecture extends known observations in the paper and is falsifiable by providing a counterexample where the graph contains a cycle.
proof_strategy: Induction on the size of S combined with combinatorial analysis of the equivalence relation; check connectivity and absence of cycles; search for counterexamples computationally.
title: Conjecture on the tree structure of T(S) for subsets of the projective line

description: This paper investigates the structural constraints under which a finite poset admits a probabilistic powerdomain isomorphic to an RB-domain. The key claim is that such a domain must inherit a least element and possess a tree-like Hasse graph structure.
proof_strategy: Constructive separation with two clear obstruction layers
title: Characterizing finite posets whose probabilistic powerdomain is an RB-domain

description: A countable FAC poset satisfies the Aharoni-Korman conjecture if and only if it does not contain a saturated chain D such that either D or its reverse is a countable direct sum of infinite co-wellfounded posets.
proof_strategy: Combine the paper's result (absence of such chains implies the conjecture) with constructing a counterexample poset lacking such chains where the conjecture fails, or proving the reverse implication via structural analysis of H(P) and scattered decompositions.
title: Characterization of the Aharoni-Korman Conjecture via Saturated Chains

description: The Ehrhart $h^*$-polynomial of a symmetric edge polytope is γ-positive if and only if the graph has a vertex connected to all other vertices.
proof_strategy: Prove that cones are γ-positive (already established) and that non-cones (e.g., series-parallel graphs) are not γ-positive (as shown by counterexamples), formalizing graph-cone characterization and polynomial coefficients in Lean 4.
title: Gamma-positivity of Symmetric Edge Polytopes is Equivalent to the Graph Being a Cone

For each divisor d|N, let w_d be the Atkin-Lehner involution on X_N, and let X_N/⟨w_d⟩ be the corresponding quotient curve. The conjecture states that the set of all such N for which there exists at least one divisor d|N such that the quotient curve X_N/⟨w_d⟩ has genus zero is exactly the finite set {6, 10, 14, 15, 21, 22, 26, 33, 34, 35, 38, 39, 46, 51, 55, 57, 58, 62, 65, 69, 74, 77, 82, 85, 86, 87, 91, 93, 94, 95, 106, 111, 115, 118, 119, 122, 123, 129, 133, 134, 141, 142, 143, 145, 146, 155, 158, 159, 161, 166, 177, 178, 183, 185, 187, 194, 201, 202, 203, 205, 206, 209, 213, 214, 215, 217, 218, 219, 221, 226, 235, 237, 247, 249, 253, 254, 259, 262, 265, 267, 274, 278, 287, 291, 295, 298, 299, 301, 302, 303, 305, 309, 314, 319, 321, 323, 326, 327, 329, 334, 335, 339, 341, 346, 355, 358, 362, 365, 371, 377, 381, 382, 386, 391, 393, 394, 395, 398, 403, 407, 411, 413, 415, 417, 422, 427, 437, 445, 446, 447, 451, 453, 454, 458, 466, 469, 471, 473, 478, 481, 482, 485, 489, 493, 497}. (This list is conjectural and based on known classifications of genus-zero Atkin-Lehner quotients of Shimura curves.)
proof_strategy: Use the genus formula for Atkin-Lehner quotients of Shimura curves, which expresses the genus in terms of class numbers of quaternion orders, fixed point counts of the Atkin-Lehner involutions, and contributions from elliptic points. Systematically evaluate this formula for all squarefree N with an even number of prime factors, leveraging known bounds on class numbers to prove finiteness of the genus-zero cases. The computation reduces to checking a finite list of N up to a computable bound, which can be verified by computer-assisted enumeration of the genus formula.
title: Classification of Genus-Zero Atkin-Lehner Quotients of Shimura Curves

description: The conjecture predicts that a graph with maximum degree exceeding one-third of its vertex count must contain a Δ(G)-overfull subgraph, linking colorable constraints to structural thresholds.

title: Towards the Overfull Conjecture II

description: For any graph G with Δ(G) ≥ (1/3 + 1)|V(G)|, χ'(G) = Δ(G) if and only if G contains no Δ(G)-overfull subgraph.
proof_strategy: Utilizing combinatorial methods such as matching polytope theorems or extremal graph theory to establish the necessary conditions for the chromatic index based on overfull subgraphs.
title: Overfull Conjecture with Tightened Degree Condition

description: Let P be a finite poset. The main theorem shows that V₁(P) is an RB-domain iff P has a least element and its undirected Hasse graph is a tree. I conjecture that the four-point diamond (a poset with 4 elements where 2 incomparable elements are both below 2 incomparable maxima) is the unique minimal poset violating this: any finite poset P with fewer than 4 elements has V₁(P) an RB-domain, and among 4-element posets, only the four-point diamond violates the RB-domain property. This is falsifiable by either finding a smaller counterexample or proving no other 4-element poset violates the condition.
proof_strategy: 1) Enumerate all finite posets with ≤3 elements and verify V₁(P) is always RB-domain using the known characterization. 2) Classify all 4-element posets and compute their undirected Hasse graphs. 3) Show that only the four-point diamond has both a least element and a cyclic Hasse graph (specifically, a 4-cycle). 4) Apply the local stochastic cone non-simpliciality argument to prove RB-domain failure for this case.
title: Uniqueness of the Four-Point Diamond as Minimal RB-Domain Violator in Probabilistic Powerdomains

description: Conjecture: Let (V,Q) be a non‑degenerate quadratic space over a finite field 𝔽_q with q>3 odd. Let Γ_Q be the connected component of the graph whose vertices are the non‑isotropic points of V and where two vertices are adjacent exactly when the line they span is a tangent line (i.e. contains a unique isotropic point). Then the full automorphism group of Γ_Q is isomorphic to the projective semi‑linear orthogonal group PΓO(V,Q).
proof_strategy: Use the local characterization theorem (Theorem 1 in the paper) to show that any graph automorphism of Γ_Q induces an automorphism of the associated tangent geometry (points = non‑isotropic points, lines = tangent lines). Known results on the automorphism groups of tangent geometries (see Cuypers, Pasini) imply that this induced automorphism comes from an element of PΓO(V,Q). Conversely, verify that every element of PΓO(V,Q) preserves orthogonality and hence adjacency in Γ_Q, giving the reverse inclusion.
title: Automorphism group of the orthogonal graph Γ_Q equals the projective semi‑linear orthogonal group

description: The transformation matrix encoding the change of the h-vector of a simplicial complex under the r-colored barycentric subdivision is totally positive (all minors are non-negative). The paper establishes that this matrix is TP_2, and this conjecture posits that the stronger total positivity (TP) property holds, extending the confirmed TP property of the standard barycentric and interval subdivisions.
proof_strategy: Extend the combinatorial network representation or the sufficient conditions for total positivity used for the barycentric and interval subdivisions to the r-colored barycentric subdivision. This may involve verifying the Whitney conditions or finding a suitable planar network whose path-generating function equals the transformation matrix entries.
title: Total positivity of the r-colored barycentric subdivision transformation matrix

description: For an odd prime p, let n = (p-1)/2 and χ be the Legendre symbol modulo p. For a ∈ F_p^×, define D_a(0) = det_{1 ≤ i,j ≤ n}(χ(i^2 - a*j)). Then D_a(0) = 0 if and only if p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and χ(a * n!) = 1.
proof_strategy: Define the Legendre symbol and the matrix M over the integers. Show that the determinant of M vanishes under the stated conditions by applying row and column operations to relate the determinant to the Pfaffian of an associated skew-symmetric matrix, leveraging properties of quadratic residues modulo p.
title: Vanishing Criterion for Legendre Symbol Determinants

description: For every connected simple graph G of order at least three, the independence number α(G) is bounded below by the sum of the annihilation number a(G) and the Havel-Hakimi residue res(G), divided by the maximum degree Δ(G). That is, α(G) ≥ (a(G) + res(G)) / Δ(G), or equivalently, α(G) * Δ(G) ≥ a(G) + res(G).
proof_strategy: Formalize the annihilation number, Havel-Hakimi residue, and maximum degree for simple graphs. Construct annihilating decompositions and prove the edge count inequality e(A) ≤ e(B) for the partition. Combine this with the classical Havel-Hakimi residue inequality res(G) ≤ α(G) and the Caro-Wei bounds to establish the multiplicative inequality.
title: TxGraffiti Annihilation-Residue Inequality

description: For all positive integers m and n, the number of intervals in the greedy m-Tamari poset on m-Dyck paths of semi-length n equals the number of rooted planar (m+1)-constellations with n black faces. This generalizes the m=1 case proven in the paper (where greedy Tamari intervals are equinumerous to bipartite planar maps, i.e., 2-constellations) and remains open for m ≥ 2.
proof_strategy: The m=1 proof establishes a recursive decomposition isomorphism between greedy Tamari intervals and bipartite planar maps. For general m, one would need to: (1) formalize m-Dyck paths and the greedy m-Tamari poset cover relation; (2) define planar (m+1)-constellations; (3) establish that both families satisfy isomorphic recursive decomposition schemes; (4) conclude equinumerosity by induction. The refined conjecture additionally tracks the number of vertices of degree m+1 in the constellation and the number of ascents of the lower bound of the interval.
title: Equinumerosity of greedy m-Tamari intervals and planar (m+1)-constellations

description: For any real t ≥ 3, the absolute value of the Riemann zeta function on the 1-line is bounded by 1/2 log t + 1.57. This formalizes the primary improved 'trivial' bound from the paper using smoothing techniques, bypassing the need for exponential sum arguments for smaller values of t.
proof_strategy: Formalize the smooth approximation of zeta(1+it) using the exponential sum with the kernel exp(-n/X). Decompose the sum, bound the error terms using bounds on |zeta(1/2+it)|, and optimize the parameter X to derive the explicit constant 1.57.
title: Explicit Upper Bound on the Riemann Zeta Function on the 1-Line via Smoothing

description: For any d-dimensional spanning k-tree K contained in the join V₁*⋯*V_{d+1} and any affine map A:|Δ_V|→ℝ^d with 0∈A(V_i) for all i, there exists a face σ∈K with 0∈A(σ) such that the number of faces in K is bounded by a polynomial in |V| of degree at most k+1. Moreover, when k=1 (spanning trees), the bound is linear in |V|.
proof_strategy: Construct explicit minimal subcomplexes using induction on k, leveraging the recursive structure of spanning k-trees where each k-tree can be built from a (k-1)-tree by adding a spanning tree structure. Apply the known result for k=0 (bipartite case) recursively while maintaining the polynomial bound through careful counting of faces in the iterated join construction.
title: Colorful Carathéodory theorem for spanning k-trees admits a polynomial-size witness

description: The paper proves an edge-spectral supersaturation bound with a sharp constant $B_F$ for color-critical graphs $F$ with $\chi(F) \ge 4$. A natural open problem is whether the same bound holds for $\chi(F) = 3$, most notably for triangles ($K_3$). The conjecture states that for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exist $\delta > 0$ and $M$ such that for all $m \ge M$ and $0 < q \le \delta \sqrt{m}$, any graph $G$ with $m$ edges and $\lambda^2(G) \ge m + q$ contains at least $(1 - \epsilon) q \sqrt{m}$ triangles, corresponding to the sharp constant $B_{K_3} = 1$.
proof_strategy: Adapt the spectral stability methods used for $\chi(F) \ge 4$ to the $\chi(F)=3$ case. This requires establishing spectral stability for near-bipartite graphs, then applying supersaturation counting arguments within the bipartite structure to find the requisite number of triangles. The bipartite case $r=2$ might require different spectral inequalities or combinatorial reductions since the Li-Liu-Zhang bound was only for $r \ge 3$.
title: Edge-Spectral Supersaturation for Triangles

description: The generalized honeymoon Oberwolfach problem HOP(2^{⟨s⟩}, 2m), which seats 2n participants (with n = s + m) at s tables of size 2 and one round table of size 2m such that each participant sits next to their spouse every time and next to each other participant exactly once, has a solution if and only if s > 0 or m is even.
proof_strategy: Formalize the necessary graph-theoretic definitions for 4-fold graphs and HOP decompositions. Prove the equivalence between the seating problem and the graph decomposition problem (Theorem 3.2). Establish base cases by formalizing Lemma 3.3 (for odd m) and Lemma 3.4 (for even m). Construct the general solution by inductively building decompositions for larger n by extending the graph using 1-regular subgraph decompositions (Lemma 3.5 and Lemma 3.6).
title: Complete Solution to the Generalized Honeymoon Oberwolfach Problem with One Round Table

description: For every finite poset P of width at most 2, the Ehrhart h*-polynomial h*(O(P); t) of the order polytope O(P) is real-rooted. This extends the paper's result for generalized snake posets (a proper subclass of width-two posets) to all width-two posets, and would unify real-rootedness phenomena observed across flow polytopes, rook polynomials, and P-Eulerian polynomials for this entire width regime.
proof_strategy: Decompose an arbitrary width-two poset into a union of chains and analyze how its Jordan-Hölder set and P-Eulerian polynomial relate to a generalized non-nesting rook polynomial on an associated Ferrers diagram. The key obstacle is that arbitrary width-two posets need not be generalized snake posets, so the existing rook polynomial correspondence must be extended to handle arbitrary interleavings of two chains, possibly via interlacing root arguments or real-rootedness-preserving operations on the associated generating polynomials.
title: Real-rootedness of h*-polynomials for width-two order polytopes

description: The paper establishes the upper bound $f_{F,G}(n) \le C(\log n)^{\beta_F}$ for $r$-uniform hypergraphs. This conjecture proposes that this bound is asymptotically tight, meaning there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $f_{F,G}(n) \ge c(\log n)^{\beta_F}$ for any non-empty $r$-graph $F$ and $2$-tightly connected $r$-graph $G$ with no homomorphism from $G$ to $F$, thereby completely determining the polylogarithmic exponent $\beta_F$.
proof_strategy: Construct $G$-free hypergraphs using probabilistic methods, such as the random greedy algorithm or altered random structures, and analyze their induced $F$-free subgraphs. The analysis would require establishing isoperimetric inequalities on the 2-shadow $\partial_2F$ to demonstrate that any large enough induced subgraph must contain a copy of $F$, yielding the matching lower bound.
title: Matching Lower Bound for Generalized Erdős–Rogers Functions

description: The minimal absolute value σ₅(n) of a non-vanishing sum of n fifth roots of unity is monotone non-increasing over congruence classes of n modulo 5. Furthermore, a strict decrease σ₅(n) > σ₅(n+5) occurs if and only if n+5 is of the form 5Fₘ, Lₘ, or 2Lₘ for some positive integer m, where Fₘ and Lₘ denote the m-th Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, respectively.
proof_strategy: Define the function σ₅(n) as the infimum of the absolute values of non-vanishing sums of n 5th roots of unity. Prove the monotonicity within congruence classes modulo 5 by constructing appropriate sums. Characterize the strict decreases by relating the problem to rational approximations of the golden ratio via continued fractions, using the specific properties of Fibonacci and Lucas numbers.
title: Monotonicity and Jumps of Minimal Absolute Values of Fifth Roots of Unity Sums

description: For the morphisms $\phi$ (where $\phi(a)=abc, \phi(b)=ac, \phi(c)=b$) and $\mu$ (where $\mu(a)=a, \mu(b)=b, \mu(c)=cbbbc$), let $x'_k = \phi^k(a)$ and $x_k = \mu(x'_k)$.
