description: We conjecture that for integers l>0 and m≥1, and any prime p not dividing l+1 or (l+1 choose 2), the congruence ∑_{n=1}^{p-1}((-1)^{mn}/n^{m-1})S_l^{(m)}(n) ≡ 0 (mod p²) holds, strengthening the main theorem which only guarantees congruence modulo p. This generalizes the known m=2, l=4 case to arbitrary l and m.
proof_strategy: Use p-adic analysis and properties of multinomial coefficients modulo prime powers, potentially relating to generalized hypergeometric functions and their p-integrality properties. The approach would involve analyzing the generating function of S_l^{(m)}(n) and applying p-adic differential equations.
title: Strengthened Congruence for Generalized Multinomial Sums Modulo p²

description: For any intersecting-union family $\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^{[n]}$ and $p \in [0,1]$, define the p-biased Lubell sum as $\Lambda_p(\mathcal{F}) = \sum_{F \in \mathcal{F}} \binom{n}{|F|}^{-1} p^{|F|}(1-p)^{n-|F|}$. We conjecture that the maximum value of $\Lambda_p(\mathcal{F})$ over all IU-families is achieved uniquely (up to isomorphism) by either the family of all $(n/2)$-subsets containing a fixed element, or by a specific two-layered construction when $n$ is odd, and that the continuous integration $\int_0^1 \Lambda_p(\mathcal{F}) dp$ recovers the exact bound $\frac{n+1}{6}$ only when these extremal structures are present.
proof_strategy: Characterize the optimizer of the variational problem via Lagrange multipliers on the Boolean lattice, establish convexity properties of the p-biased measure under IU constraints, and prove uniqueness of extremal families through exchange arguments and majorization theory.
title: Exact characterization of p-biased Lubell maxima for IU-families

description: For all integers n ≥ 2, the value of b₂(n) is equal to ⌈n/2⌉ if n ≡ 0, 1, or 7 modulo 8, and equal to ⌈n/2⌉ + 1 otherwise. This conjecture formalizes the resolved cases in the paper and provides a complete characterization of b₂(n) for all n.
proof_strategy: The proof would involve verifying the modular conditions and leveraging the lower bound from Buchanan et al. combined with constructive upper bounds. By analyzing the structure of bicliques and their symmetric differences, one can show that the conjectured values are achievable and minimal.
title: Conjecture on the exact values of b₂(n) for all n

This refines the spectral analogue of the Erdős Matching Conjecture and is falsifiable by providing a counterexample for some n below the threshold or by showing non-uniqueness of the extremal structure.
proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by first establishing a shifting invariance, then applying variational estimates for the tensor spectral radius, and finally performing a saturation analysis to identify the extremal configuration; this mirrors the strategy outlined in the paper but isolates the key inequality for independent verification.
title: Spectral Extremal Conjecture for r-Uniform Hypergraphs with Bounded Matching Number

Establish the upper bound by describing an explicit algorithm that transforms any vertex to any other in at most n−2 steps, via a greedy reduction of mismatched labels, and prove its correctness by induction on n.

description: Conjecture that a set of positive integers S is sparse if and only if for every ε > 0, there exists a constant C_ε such that for all sufficiently large k, the ratio of consecutive elements in the increasing sequence s_1 < s_2 < ... satisfies s_{i+1}/s_i < C_ε(1 + ε)^i for some computable function relating to the sparsity exponent ρ. This would provide a computable characterization of sparseness that bridges the analytic definition with algorithmic computability properties used in the construction of normal numbers.

The proof would require delicate counting arguments and optimization over the parameter ρ.
title: Characterization of sparse sets via consecutive gap growth rates

title: Equality Conditions for the Fishburn Inequality for Linear Extensions of Posets

title: Unconditional Tightness of f-Degree Fault Tolerant Spanner Bounds

This captures the maximal possible order of the sum of distinct prime factors in a block of \(y\) consecutive integers.

In a formal development, the plan is to (i) define \(\omega\) and \(W\) in Lean, (ii) prove elementary bounds (e.g., \(\omega(n)\le \log n/\log\log n\)), (iii) encode the limsup condition via a universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon>0\) and an existence statement for infinitely many \(x\), and (iv) attempt a contradiction proof assuming a larger limsup.
title: Precise asymptotic for the sum of distinct prime divisors over intervals

We conjecture the stronger statement that any prime graph whose induced-{P4}-packing treewidth is at most 1 must be split. This connects the new tree-decomposition parameter to classical split graph characterization and can be formalized in Lean 4 with standard graph definitions.
proof_strategy: Formalize definitions of induced-H-packing treewidth, prime graph (no nontrivial modules), and split graph (vertices partitionable into clique and independent set). Then attempt to prove by constructing a tree decomposition with width 1 and deriving a vertex not in any induced P4 via bag properties, or search for finite counterexamples using Lean's computational capabilities and mathlib's graph library.
title: Prime graphs with induced-P4-packing treewidth at most 1 are split

description:
For a cuspidal automorphic representation \(\pi\) of \(\PGL_2\) over the function field \(F\) of a smooth projective curve \(X\) with conductor equal to an arbitrary effective divisor \(\Sigma\), the \(r\)-th derivative at the central point of the Forbes–Jones base‑change \(L\)-function \(L_{F'/F}(\pi,s)\) is (up to an explicit constant depending only on local data at \(\Sigma\) and the chosen Haar measures) equal to the self‑intersection number of the Heegner‑Drinfeld cycle \(Z_{\pi}^{r}\) inside the integral model of the moduli stack of \(\PGL_2\)-shtukas with \(\Gamma_0(\Sigma)\) level structure and supersingular legs at a fixed set of infinite places. In other words, there exists a constant \(C assemblies(r,\Sigma)\in\Q^\times\) such that
\[
\langle Z_{\pi}^{r},Z_{\pi}^{r}\rangle
= C\bigl(r,\Sigma\bigr)\cdot L_{F'/F}^{(r)}(\pi,\tfrac12).\n\]
The conjecture is formulated for all integers \(r\ge 1\) and all finite – but not necessarily square‑free – divisors \(\Sigma\).
proof_strategy: The strategy combines the geometric Satake equivalence on the moduli stack of shtukas with deeper level structure, the geometric trace formula for the relative trace of the unramified Hecke algebra, and an analysis of the deformation theory of the Heegner‑Drinfeld cycle inside the integral model. One first constructs a canonical class \([Z_{\pi}^{r}]\) in the Chow group of the integral stack for any non‑square‑free level \(\Sigma\), then shows that the cycle class satisfies a Lefschetz trace formula relating its self‑intersection to a weighted orbital integral. Using the explicit description of the weighted orbital integral in terms of the local components of \(\pi\) at the points of \(\Sigma\), one reduces the global identity to the local comparison of test functions, which is established via a local Waldspurger–Gross–Zagier lemma for the deeper parahoric level. Finally, a global spectral expansion produces the derivative of the base‑change \(L\)-function on contactar side, yielding t
title: Higher Gross‑Zagier Formula for Non‑Square‑Free Level on Shtukas

description: Conjecture: Let G be a finite toroidal bipartite graph and G' the non‑bipartite graph obtained from G by replacing every degree‑3 vertex by a triangular gadget as defined in the paper. Then the Newton polygon of the characteristic polynomial of G' coincides exactly with the Newton polygon of the characteristic polynomial of G. Moreover, the primitive edge vectors of this common polygon correspond to the homology classes of the zig‑zag cycles of G (and hence of G').
domain_bridges: Topological Graph Theory (homology of cycles on the torus)
proof_strategy: Develop a combinatorial description of the characteristic polynomial via Kasteleyn matrices for G and G'. Show that the triangle replacement amounts to multiplying the Kasteleyn matrix by a block‑diagonal matrix whose determinant contributes only a monomial factor, leaving the support of the polynomial unchanged. Use homological analysis of zig‑zag paths to identify edge normals, then invoke the known correspondence for bipartite graphs to conclude equality of Newton polygons. Formalisation can proceed by defining torus graphs, Kasteleyn orientations, and the map from perfect matchings to homology classes in Lean, then proving the determinant factorisation and support invariance.
title: Newton polygon invariance under triangle replacement in torus dimer graphs

description: For every fixed integer t ≥ 2 there exists a constant C(t)=4·t such that any graph G either contains k vertex‑disjoint, pairwise anti‑adjacent copies of the long theta Θ_t as induced minors, or there exists a set X⊆V(G) with |X|≤C(t)·k·log k whose closed neighbourhood meets every Θ_t‑induced minor of G.
proof_strategy: Use a short t‑model of the ΘZero graph together with a monotone guidance that always selects a big component of weight >½; apply the Dominated Guided Separator lemma to obtain a separator of size O(tk log k) and argue that its closed neighbourhood hits all Θ_t‑induced minors.
title: Conjecture on the size of hitting sets for Θ_t-induced minors

description:
We conjecture that the combinatorial condition defining reflected bounded‑growth tuples can be expressed solely by simple linear inequalities and parity constraints on a weakly increasing integer sequence.  In other words, for a tuple \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n\) the following are equivalent:

1. \(a\) is a reflected bounded‑growth tuple (as defined in the paper).
2. \(a\) is weakly increasing, satisfies \(a_i\le 2i-1\) for all \(i\), and has parity condition \(a_i\equiv i-1\pmod 2\) whenever \(i\) is odd.

Consequently the map \(a\mapsto\prod_{i=1}^n[ a_i+1 ]_q\) gives a bijection between such tuples and the palindromic Poincaré polynomials of type \(B_n\) which do not lie in the image of Stembridge's bottom map from type \(A_{n+1}\).  This yields a purely elementary description of the complete list of palindromic Poincaré polynomials in type \(B\).
proof_strategy:
We will formalise the conjecture in Lean 4 by defining the predicate \`is_reflected_bounded_growth\` on vectors of natural numbers, the monotonicity and inequality/parity conditions, and the associated product of \(q\)-integers.  The plan is:

1. Implement the definitions in Lean.
2. Compute the set of tuples satisfying the linear/parity characterisation for small ranks (e.g., \(n\le 8\)) and compare with the known list of reflected bounded‑growth tuples extracted from the paper (via brute‑force enumeration).
3. Use the verification for small \(n\) to gain confidence, then attempt an inductive proof that exploits the recursive structure of \(B_n\) and the relationship with the bottom map from \(A_{n+1}\).

The final theorem will assert the equivalence described above.
title: Characterizing reflected bounded‑growth tuples in type B

description: For all integers x ≥ 2 and integers u satisfying ⌊√x⌋ < u < x, the Mertens function M(x) = ∑_{n≤x} μ(n) satisfies the recursive identity M(x) = ∑_{k=1}^{⌊x/u⌋} μ(k) S(⌊x/k⌋, u), where S(y, u) = 1 - ∑_{n=⌊y/u⌋+1}^{κ_y} M(⌊y/n⌋) + κ_y M(⌊√y⌋) - ∑_{n=1}^{⌊√y⌋} ⌊y/n⌋ μ(n) and κ_y = ⌊y/(⌊√y⌋+1)⌋. This formalizes Theorem 1 of the paper with the standard split point ν_y = ⌊√y⌋ and explicit floor operations.
proof_strategy: Start from the identity ∑_{n≤y} M(⌊y/n⌋) = 1. Split the sum at n = ⌊√y⌋ using summation by parts to express ∑_{n≤κ_y} M(⌊y/n⌋) in terms of M(⌊√y⌋) and a sum involving μ(n). Define S(y,u) by isolating the terms with n ≤ ⌊y/u⌋. Verify that ∑_{k≤y/u} M(⌊y/k⌋) = S(y,u) when ⌊√y⌋ < u. Apply the generalized Möbius inversion formula ∑_{k≤x} μ(k) G(⌊x/k⌋) = F(x) where G(y) = ∑_{k≤y/u} F(⌊y/k⌋) to obtain the result.
title: Generalized Mertens Function Recursion Identity

description: Propose the precise conjecture that for every integer n ≥ 1, any family F of subsets of [n] (represented as Fin n) that is both intersecting (every two members have non‑empty intersection) and union‑avoiding (the union of any two members is not the whole set [n]) satisfies the Lubell-type inequality ∑_{A∈F} binom(n,|A|)^{-1} ≤ (n+1)/6. This statement is falsifiable: a single counterexample for some n would disprove it.
proof_strategy: p-biased measure integration over the Boolean lattice followed by continuous integration across the bias parameter p ∈ [0,1] to recover the optimal coefficient 1/6

description: For any integer k ≥ 2, the minimum number of complete bipartite graphs needed to cover each edge of the complete graph K_{2k+1} an odd number of times is exactly k+1. This confirms Conjecture 1.2 of Buchanan et al. (2023) and determines b₂(n) for all odd n.
proof_strategy: Establish the lower bound b₂(K_{2k+1}) ≥ k+1 using the F₂-rank bound b₂(G) ≥ r₂(A_G)/2, where the adjacency matrix of K_{2k+1} over F₂ has rank 2k. For the upper bound, construct an explicit odd cover of size k+1 using finite field constructions, such as symmetric conference matrices or Paley-type graphs, leveraging the fact that 2k+1 is odd.

description: The natural gradient algorithm updates parameters theta in the direction of steepest descent on the Fisher information manifold: theta_{t+1} = theta_t - eta * G^{-1}(theta_t) * gradient L(theta_t) where G is the Fisher information matrix. This is equivalent to following the geodesic on the statistical manifold (the Riemannian manifold with metric G). Conjecture: for any optimization problem with loss function L, the natural gradient descent converges to the minimum in O(1/t) iterations, regardless of the condition number of G. This is because the natural gradient follows the geodesic, which is the shortest path on the manifold, and the path length is O(1) (bounded by the diameter of the manifold). In contrast, standard gradient descent takes O(kappa) iterations where kappa is the condition number of G. Conjecture: natural gradient descent with step size eta = 1/t achieves L(theta_t) - L(theta*) = O(1/t) for convex losses, and L(theta_t) - L(theta*) = O(exp(-t/d)) for strongly convex losses, where d is the dimension. Test: compare natural gradient descent and standard gradient descent on logistic regression with varying condition numbers, verify the convergence rates. Impact: optimization is geometry. The natural gradient is the geodesic on the Fisher manifold, and geodesics are the shortest paths.
proof_strategy: Define the statistical manifold M = {p(x|theta) : theta in R^d} with the Fisher metric G(theta) = E_{p(x|theta)}[nabla_theta log p(x|theta) nabla_theta log p(x|theta)^T]. The natural gradient is: tilde{nabla} L = G^{-1}(theta) * nabla_theta L. Natural gradient descent: theta_{t+1} = theta_t - eta_t * tilde{nabla} L(theta_t). Convergence analysis: for convex L, the natural gradient descent is equivalent to mirror descent with the Bregman divergence generated by the log-partition function. The convergence rate for mirror descent is O(1/t) for convex objectives and O(exp(-t/d)) for strongly convex objectives. Key insight: the natural gradient reparametrizes the problem so that the Fisher metric becomes the identity, 'whitening' the landscape. This is equivalent to following the geodesic on M, which is the shortest path from theta_0 to theta*. The geodesic distance d(theta_0, theta*) = O(sqrt(d)) (bounded by the diameter of the parameter space). Natural gradient descent covers this distance in O(d) steps, giving convergence rate O(exp(-1/d)). Test: implement natural gradient descent for logistic regression (where G(theta) = X^T diag(p(1-p)) X), compare with standard GD for condition numbers kappa = 1, 10, 100, 1000. Measure convergence rate L(theta_t) - L(theta*) vs t.
title: Information Geometry of Optimization: Natural Gradient Follows Geodesics

description: Prove that 2-dimensional Newtonian gravity is mathematically pathological: orbits don't close, there's no stable circular orbit, and gravitational potential is logarithmic. Formalize the Bertrand-Darboux theorem failure in 2D and prove that stable planetary systems cannot exist in Flatland.
title: Flatland Catastrophe: When 2D Physics Breaks

description: Prime gaps — the spaces between consecutive primes — are like empty cells in a crossword puzzle. The gaps are 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, 4, 6, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, ... (OEIS A001223). The pattern seems random, but the crossword has rules: (1) All prime gaps are even (except the first gap of 1 between 2 and 3). (2) A gap g can only appear at position n if n+g is prime and all of n+1, n+2, ..., n+g-1 are composite. (3) The density of gap g near n is approximately 2*C_2/(g*log(n)) where C_2 is the twin prime constant. Conjecture: The prime gap crossword is uniquely solvable — given the pattern of gaps up to N, the next prime is determined with probability 1 - O(1/log(N)). More precisely, the conditional probability that the next prime after p is p + g, given all primes up to p, is approximately 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p)) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2). This is the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for prime gaps. But the crossword has a surprise: certain gap patterns FORCE the next number. For example, if the gaps near n are 6, 4, 2, 6, then the next gap is almost certainly 4 (the only way to fill the crossword). Test: compute the conditional probabilities for prime gaps up to 10^8 and verify they match the Hardy-Littlewood prediction. Find forcing patterns (gaps that uniquely determine the next prime) and prove they occur with positive density. Impact: prime gaps are not random — they are a solvable crossword puzzle with deterministic rules.
proof_strategy: Define the prime gap sequence g(n) = p(n+1) - p(n) for n >= 1. State the Hardy-Littlewood gap conjecture: P(g(n) = g | g(n-1) = g_{-1}, ...) = 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p(n))) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2) where C_2 = 0.66016... is the twin prime constant. Define forcing patterns: a sequence of gaps g_{-k}, ..., g_{-1} is forcing if P(g(0) = g | g_{-k}, ..., g_{-1}) > 0.99 for exactly one value of g. Prove forcing patterns have positive density: the pattern [6, 4, 2, 6] is forcing because after primes p, p+6, p+10, p+12, p+18, the next prime must be p+22 with probability > 0.95 (since p+20 is even, p+21 is divisible by 3 if p ≡ 1 mod 3, etc.). Compute conditional probabilities numerically for N = 10^8. Test: enumerate forcing patterns and compute their density.
title: The Prime Number Crossword: Filling the Gaps in the Primes

description: A dataset with missing values is a sheaf on a poset: the poset is the set of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion), and the sheaf assigns to each feature subset the set of complete observations on those features. The missing data creates 'holes' in the sheaf: H^0 measures the global sections (complete observations) and H^1 measures the obstructions to patching local observations into global ones. Conjecture: For a dataset with missing rate r, the dimension of H^1 is approximately r * n * (r * log(1/r)), where n is the number of features. This means: the 'amount of missing information' grows super-linearly with the missing rate, and imputation is fundamentally harder than interpolation because H^1 > 0 means there is no consistent way to fill in the missing data. The sheaf-theoretic imputation: fill in missing values by finding the section s in H^0 that minimizes the coboundary delta(s) in H^1. This is the maximum likelihood imputation under the assumption that the data is locally consistent. Test: generate synthetic datasets with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compute H^0 and H^1 of the data sheaf, and verify dim(H^1) ~ r*n*r*log(1/r). Compare sheaf-theoretic imputation with standard methods (mean, KNN, MICE). Impact: missing data is a topological problem, and the sheaf cohomology tells you exactly how much information is lost and whether it can be recovered.
proof_strategy: Define the data sheaf: for a dataset with n features and m observations, the poset P is the set of feature subsets S subset {1,...,n} ordered by inclusion. The sheaf F assigns to each S the set of observations that have all features in S present (complete rows restricted to columns in S). The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S are projections that drop columns in S\T. Define H^0(F) = ker(delta_0) = global sections (observations complete on ALL features). Define H^1(F) = ker(delta_1)/im(delta_0) = obstructions to patching local observations into global ones. Compute delta_0 and delta_1 using the Cech complex. Estimate dim(H^1): for missing rate r and n features, each observation is missing r*n features on average. The expected number of complete observations is m*(1-r)^n (each feature present with probability 1-r). The obstruction dim(H^1) grows with the number of incompatible local patches. Each missing feature creates a potential obstruction. Estimated dim(H^1) ~ m * r * (1-(1-r)^n) ~ m * r * n * r for small r. Test: generate data from a known multivariate normal, introduce MCAR missing values at rate r, compute H^0 and H^1, fit dim(H^1) ~ C * r * n * r * log(1/r).
title: Sheaf Cohomology of Data: The Topology of Missing Information

description:
# Future Directions: Log-Concavity in the d-Hoggatt Hierarchy

This cycle established a sharp dichotomy for the *total* d-Hoggatt numbers
`H_d(n) = ∑_k H_d(n,k)`: the `d = 1` totals `2^n` are infinitely log-concave
(indeed log-linear), while the `d = 2` totals (Catalan numbers) are strictly
log-convex, and the `d = 3` totals (Baxter numbers) are empirically log-convex.
The following conjectures are the natural next targets.

## Conjecture 1 — Universal log-convexity of the totals for d ≥ 2

For every `d ≥ 2`, the total d-Hoggatt numbers are strictly log-convex:
`H_d(n+1)² < H_d(n) · H_d(n+2)` for all `n ≥ 0`.

The key insight is that each `H_d(n)` is a positively weighted sum of products
of binomial coefficients whose dominant growth ratio increases with `n`, so the
totals inherit the log-convexity of the Catalan case rather than the
log-concavity of the individual rows. Why now? The Catalan (`d = 2`) case is now
settled from a two-term recurrence, and the Baxter (`d = 3`) case matches it
term-by-term in the computed data, suggesting a single recurrence-driven
argument covers the whole family.

## Conjecture 2 — Row-sum log-convexity is a summation phenomenon

If `T(n,k)` is any triangle whose rows are log-concave and whose row-ratio
`T(n+1,k)/T(n,k)` is nondecreasing in `n`, then the row sums `S(n) = ∑_k T(n,k)`
are log-convex.

The key insight is that log-convexity of the totals is not special to Hoggatt
triangles but follows from monotone amplification of a common growth factor
across rows, a Chebyshev-sum / rearrangement effect. Why now? Having seen the
same negative discriminant `Δ_n < 0` for both Catalan and Baxter totals, the
phenomenon is clearly structural rather than coincidental and deserves a triangle
-level hypothesis.

## Conjecture 3 — Infinite log-concavity of the rows

For every `d ≥ 1`, each fixed row `k ↦ H_d(n,k)` of the d-Hoggatt triangle is
infinitely log-concave.

The key insight is that the log-concavity operator, when applied to a finite
positive log-concave row with the golden-ratio-squared safety factor
`a_k² ≥ ((3+√5)/2) · a_{k-1} a_{k+1}`, reproduces that same safety factor, so a
single closure lemma propagates through all iterates. Why now? The threshold
constant `(3+√5)/2` is exactly the fixed point of the operator's worst-case
ratio, and the toolkit built this cycle (the operator `𝓛`, its annihilation of
log-linear sequences, and closure under products) already contains the moving
parts needed to attack the closure lemma.

## Conjecture 4 — A log-concave "renormalization" of the totals

For every `d ≥ 2` there is an explicit positive normalizing sequence `w_d(n)`
(e.g. a ratio of factorials) such that the renormalized totals
`H_d(n) / w_d(n)` are infinitely log-concave, even though the raw totals are
log-convex.

The key insight is that log-convexity of the totals is caused by a smooth,
predictable growth factor which can be divided out, leaving a residual sequence
governed by the same infinite-log-concavity mechanism as the rows. Why now? The
exact growth ratio `(n+2)(2n+3)/((2n+1)(n+3))` for the Catalan totals is now
known in closed form, giving a concrete first candidate for `w_2` and a template
for higher `d`.

## Conjecture 5 — Tropical dequantization of the dichotomy

Under the tropical (min-plus) limit that sends a positive sequence `a_n` to its
valuations `v_n = −log a_n`, log-concavity becomes convexity of `v` and
log-linearity becomes affinity of `v`. The `d = 1`/`d ≥ 2` dichotomy then reads:
`v` is affine for `d = 1` and strictly concave for `d ≥ 2`.

The key insight is that the log-concavity operator degenerates, in the tropical
limit, to a second finite difference, so infinite log-concavity corresponds to a
sequence of iterated finite differences retaining a fixed sign — a purely
piecewise-linear, tropical-geometric condition. Why now? Casting the numeric
dichotomy in the min-plus semiring links this combinatorial question to tropical
convexity, where second-difference sign conditions are the natural objects and
powerful piecewise-linear tools are available.
title: Sharp dichotomy for the *total* d-Hoggatt numbers

# Future Directions

The Lean development `Catalog/MachineLearning/KnottedLightAlexander.lean` formalizes
the exact algebra behind the "knotted light" OAM/Alexander-polynomial conjecture for
the four smallest knots. Natural extensions:

1. **Cyclotomic identification.**  Prove `trefoilPoly = cyclotomic 6 ℤ` and
   `cinquefoilPoly = cyclotomic 10 ℤ` directly in Mathlib (rather than only proving
   the individual root facts). This would make the "roots are exactly the primitive
   n-th roots of unity" statement complete, including the *converse* (no spurious
   roots) via `Polynomial.roots_cyclotomic`.

2. **Torus-knot family.**  The trefoil and cinquefoil are the `(2, 3)` and `(2, 5)`
   torus knots, with `Δ_{(2,2k+1)}(t) = (t^{2k+1} + 1)/(t + 1)`. Formalize the general
   torus-knot Alexander polynomial and show its roots are the `(4k+2)`-th roots of
   unity that are not `(2k+1)`-th roots — a uniform generalization of the two cases
   proved here.

3. **General reciprocity and `Δ(1) = ±1`.**  State and prove the reciprocity law
   `t^{2g} Δ(1/t) = Δ(t)` and the normalization `Δ(1) = ±1` from an abstract
   axiomatization of Alexander polynomials (e.g. via Seifert matrices `V`,
   `Δ(t) = det(V − t Vᵀ)`), instead of case by case.

4. **Knot determinant as `|Δ(−1)|`.**  Connect the numbers `3, 5, 5` proved here to
   the determinant defined through a Goeritz or Seifert matrix, and to
   `p`-colorability (`3`-colorable ⇔ `3 ∣ det`).

5. **Off-circle roots and the golden ratio.**  Generalize the figure-eight
   observation: characterize which knots have all Alexander roots on the unit circle
   (a necessary condition for genuine root-of-unity OAM quantization). The
   figure-eight, with roots `φ^{±2}`, is the smallest knot violating this.
title: The Lean development `Catalog/MachineLearning/KnottedLightAlexander.lean` formal

description:
# Future Directions: The Geometry and Universal Structure of Surprise

This cycle established two complementary pillars. First, *surprise* — the gap between
the most conservative and most divergent resolution of a setup — is a genuine
geometric invariant equal to the diameter of the resolution configuration
(nonnegative, vanishing exactly on constant setups, monotone under refinement, and
attained). Second, when a *canonical* (terminal) resolution exists, it is unique in the
strongest possible sense: up to a unique, coherent isomorphism, and it is rigid. The
following conjectures push both pillars further.

## 1. Surprise as a genuine metric diameter in higher dimensions

**Conjecture.** For a finite configuration of resolutions embedded in a Euclidean space
of any dimension, the natural surprise invariant equals the metric diameter of the
configuration's convex hull, and it remains monotone under enrichment and subadditive
under overlays of setups.

**The key insight is** that the one-dimensional identity "surprise = range = greatest
pairwise distance" is not special to the line: it is a shadow of the general fact that
the extreme spread of a compact configuration is realised on its boundary.

**Why now?** The one-dimensional case is fully settled here with an attained diameter
characterisation, giving an exact template — extremal witnesses plus a uniform bound —
that generalises verbatim once "endpoints" are replaced by "hull vertices."

## 2. A vanishing dichotomy separating puns from absurdism

**Conjecture.** The surprise invariant admits a sharp threshold: below it, every setup
is equivalent (after normalisation) to a near-constant configuration; above it, setups
necessarily contain two resolutions in "different categories" that no refinement can
reconcile.

**The key insight is** that the zero-surprise characterisation is not merely a boundary
case but the base of a stratification: distance from the constant locus measures how
far a setup has escaped its expected resolution.

**Why now?** We have proven the exact vanishing locus (surprise `0` iff all resolutions
coincide) and that surprise is monotone; a stratification by surprise value is the
immediate next quantitative refinement.

## 3. Universal resolutions as limits of refinement chains

**Conjecture.** Every setup whose resolutions form a directed refinement system admits a
universal resolution, obtained as the colimit of the refinement chain, and this colimit
is automatically rigid.

**The key insight is** that terminality — proven here to force unique, coherent,
rigidity-witnessing structure — is exactly the property a well-behaved colimit inherits,
so existence of the canonical resolution reduces to directedness of refinements.

**Why now?** The abstract uniqueness and rigidity of terminal resolutions are already in
hand; the only missing ingredient for a general existence theorem is a construction, and
directed colimits supply the standard one.

## 4. Sharp stability of surprise under perturbation

**Status.** The basic stability estimate is now settled: perturbing every resolution of
a setup by at most `ε` changes its surprise by at most `2ε`. This confirms that surprise
is a robust invariant — small changes in how each resolution is read cannot produce a
large change in humor.

**Conjecture (next step).** The factor `2` is optimal, and more is true: surprise is a
contraction under any reinterpretation that is itself a contraction of the resolution
axis, and the estimate composes — a chain of `k` perturbations of sizes `ε₁, …, ε_k`
moves surprise by at most `2(ε₁ + ⋯ + ε_k)`, with equality achieved on suitably
"stretched" two-point setups.

**The key insight is** that surprise is built from two extremal selectors, each of which
moves by at most the perturbation size, so their difference is controlled — and that the
worst case is realised precisely when the two extremes are pushed apart in opposite
directions, which pins down the sharp constant.

**Why now?** The extremal (`IsGreatest`/`IsLeast`) characterisations of the two canonical
resolutions, together with the just-established `2ε` stability bound, are exactly the
ingredients needed to identify the extremal configurations that make the constant sharp.
title: Two complementary pillars. First, *surprise* — the gap be

# Future Directions — The Topology of Arithmetic

This cycle established that the zero-dimensional persistent barcode of the prime
point cloud on the line is exactly the sequence of prime gaps, and that the twin
prime conjecture is the assertion that a length-`2` bar recurs forever.  The
following conjectures push the program further.

## 1. The gap-value spectrum is the set of barcode step-points

**Conjecture.** For the prime point cloud, the set of scales at which the number
of connected components strictly decreases equals the set of values attained by
the gap sequence, and each even number `2k` that occurs as a gap contributes a
positive-density family of bars of that exact death scale.

*The key insight is* that on a line the barcode is a lossless recording of the
gap multiset, so distributional questions about prime gaps (Polignac-type
statements) become questions about the multiplicity of individual bar lengths.

*Why now?* The single-linkage characterisation proved this cycle turns "how many
gaps equal `2k`" into "how many bars have death scale `2k`", making every result
on gap frequencies immediately a statement about barcode multiplicities.

## 2. A persistence-stability form of the average gap law

**Conjecture.** The empirical distribution of the first `N` finite `H_0` bar
lengths, rescaled by `log p_N`, converges to a fixed limiting profile; in
particular the mean bar length is asymptotic to `log p_N`.

*The key insight is* that the average bar length over the first `N` primes equals
`(p_N − p_1)/N`, a telescoping identity, so the prime number theorem controls the
first moment of the barcode directly.

*Why now?* With the barcode identified with the gap sequence, the mean-length
statement is exactly `(p_{N+1} − 2)/N → ` the average gap, and only the higher
moments and the shape of the limiting profile remain open.

## 3. Higher homology from the two-dimensional prime lattice

**Conjecture.** Embedding primes as the planar cloud `p_n ↦ (p_n, p_{n+1})` and
running the Rips filtration produces a first non-trivial `H_1` class whose birth
scale is governed by admissible gap patterns `(g_n, g_{n+1})`, and the shortest
persistent loop corresponds to the smallest admissible triple of consecutive
gaps.

*The key insight is* that genuine one-dimensional holes require at least three
points arranged non-collinearly, which on the gap side means a constraint on
consecutive gap *pairs* rather than single gaps.

*Why now?* The one-dimensional theory is now fully understood, so the natural
next obstruction — the first appearance of `H_1` — isolates exactly the
combinatorics of consecutive-gap patterns, a well-studied but topologically
unexploited object.

## 4. Barcode rigidity distinguishes primes from random gap models

**Conjecture.** The prime barcode differs measurably from that of a Poisson point
process of matching local intensity: the fraction of length-`2` bars stays
bounded away from the Poisson prediction, detectable purely from the barcode.

*The key insight is* that twin primes are anomalously frequent compared with a
memoryless gap model, and this anomaly survives as a persistent statistical
signature in the length-`2` bar count.

*Why now?* The exact identification of length-`2` bars with twin pairs gives a
clean, model-free statistic on which prime and Poisson barcodes can be compared
head to head.
title: That the zero-dimensional persistent barcode of the prime

# Future Directions

This project formalises the *algebraic skeleton* of the "topology of Bach"
mission: pitch-class space as `ℤ/12ℤ`, harmonic cycles as cyclic subgroups, and
the circle of fifths as the unique-up-to-symmetry longest such cycle. What is
proved is a self-contained, machine-checked chain:

1. `cycleLen_eq` — harmonic cycle length `= 12 / gcd(12, k)`.
2. Concrete values (fifth `12`, tritone `2`, third `3`, whole tone `6`, …).
3. `cycleLen_le`, `fifth_cycleLen_maximal`, `cycleLen_dvd_12` — the fifth is a
   longest cycle; every cycle length divides `12`.
4. `cycleLen_eq_12_iff`, `maximal_generators` — spanning intervals are exactly
   those coprime to `12`, namely `{1, 5, 7, 11}`.
5. `fifth_generates`, `generates_iff` — the fifth generates the whole
   pitch-class group; generation ⇔ coprimality.
6. `cof_hamiltonian` — the explicit circle of fifths is a Hamiltonian cycle.
7. `barLen`, `fifth_barLen_gt_half`, `tritone_barLen_lt_half` — the mission's
   normalised persistence-bar thresholds (Bach `> 0.5`, atonal `< 0.5`).

## Natural next steps

- **Genuine persistent homology.** Replace the proxy `cycleLen` with an actual
  Vietoris–Rips filtration on a finite metric pitch-class space (the "torus"
  metric `d(a,b) = min(|a-b|, 12-|a-b|)` on `ℤ/12ℤ`, or a weighted graph metric
  along fifths). Prove that `H₁` of the Rips complex is non-trivial at the scale
  where the circle-of-fifths cycle appears, and compute its birth/death. Mathlib
  now has simplicial/`SimplicialComplex` machinery to build on.

- **Betti numbers of circulant graphs.** The interval-`k` harmonic motion is a
  circulant graph `Cay(ℤ/12ℤ, {±k})`; its cycle structure and first Betti number
  `b₁ = |E| - |V| + (# components)` can be computed group-theoretically. Formalise
  `b₁` for these graphs and connect it to `cycleLen`.

- **Other temperaments.** Everything generalises from `12` to arbitrary `n`-tone
  equal temperament (`ℤ/nℤ`): the longest harmonic cycle has length `n`, attained
  exactly by intervals coprime to `n` (there are `φ(n)` of them). A parametrised
  version of `IntervalCycles.lean` over `ℤ/nℤ` would state and prove this in full
  generality (19-TET, 31-TET, etc.).

- **Voice-leading geometry.** Encode chords (not just single intervals) as
  multisets of pitch classes and study the orbifold `Tⁿ/Sₙ` of Tymoczko's
  voice-leading spaces; the circle of fifths reappears as a geodesic loop.

- **Empirical bridge.** Connect the normalised `barLen` thresholds to a real
  persistence computation over corpora (Bach chorales vs. pop vs. atonal),
  closing the loop with the mission's stated experiment.
title: This project formalises the *algebraic skeleton* of the "topology of Bach"

# Stochastic Galois Theory over Finite Fields — Results and Future Directions

## What was proved (all `sorry`-free, axioms `propext`/`Classical.choice`/`Quot.sound`)

**`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisRoots.lean` — the expected-roots identity.**
For a monic degree-`n` polynomial over a finite commutative ring `K` (`q = |K|`, `n ≥ 1`),
encoded by its coefficient vector `v : Fin n → K`,
```
∑ v, #{ r : K | monicEval n v r = 0 } = q^n            (total_root_incidences)
```
i.e. **the expected number of roots of a uniformly random monic degree-`n` polynomial is
exactly `1`**. The proof is a clean double count: swap the sum over polynomials with the
sum over base points, and observe that for a fixed `r` exactly `q^{n-1}` polynomials
vanish at `r` (the constant coefficient is forced). A specialization
`total_root_incidences_zmod` phrases it over `F_p`.

This is the cleanest universally-true instance of the "random polynomial = random
permutation" dictionary: roots ↔ linear factors ↔ **fixed points of the Frobenius
permutation**, and a uniform permutation in `S_n` also has exactly one fixed point on
average.

**`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisDegreeTwo.lean` — exact degree-2 statistics.**
Over a finite field `K` of odd characteristic (`q = |K|`):
```
2 · #{ reducible quadratics }   = q(q+1)                (card_reducible)
2 · #{ irreducible quadratics } = q(q-1)                (card_irreducible)
#{ quadratics with a repeated root } = q                (card_double_root)
```
proved from the two structural facts `sum_nroots` (total incidences `= q^2`) and
`nroots_le_two` (a quadratic has `≤ 2` roots), via completing the square
(`nroots_eq_disc`) and the square-root count lemmas. Consequences: proportion irreducible
`→ 1/2` (the `S_2` `2`-cycle fraction) and proportion with vanishing discriminant `= 1/q`.

**`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisCyclic.lean` — a structural correction.**
```
IsEmpty ((L ≃ₐ[K] L) ≃* Equiv.Perm (Fin n))   for finite L and n ≥ 3   (finiteField_gal_ne_symm)
```
Over a finite field every Galois group is cyclic (Frobenius), hence abelian, hence never
isomorphic to the non-abelian `S_n` for `n ≥ 3`. The prompt's conjecture that
`P(Gal = S_n) → 1` is therefore false at the group-theoretic level: `P(Gal = S_n) = 0`
for `n ≥ 3`. What survives is the *cycle-type/factorization* heuristic, not the
"maximal group" one.

## The corrected picture

Over `ℚ`, Hilbert irreducibility gives `Gal = S_n` for almost all polynomials. Over `F_q`
this fails: Galois groups are cyclic. The right analogue is **Frobenius equidistribution**
— the factorization type of a random monic degree-`n` polynomial (the cycle type of
Frobenius on the roots) is distributed like the cycle type of a uniform random permutation
in `S_n` as `q → ∞`. The proved theorems are the two cleanest exact cases of this:
the fixed-point count in all degrees, and the complete `n = 2` distribution.

## Concrete next steps

1. **Degree-3 full distribution.** Prove `#{irreducible monic cubics} = (q^3 - q)/3` and
   the split of reducible cubics into `(x-r)(x-s)(x-t)` types, matching the `S_3` cycle
   distribution `{3-cycles : 1/3, transpositions : 1/2, identity : 1/6}` in the limit. The
   incidence method here generalizes: also count `∑ (#roots choose 2)` to access pair
   statistics.

2. **Gauss's formula in general.** Formalize `I_q(n) = (1/n) ∑_{d|n} μ(d) q^{n/d}` for the
   number of monic irreducibles of degree `n` over `F_q`, giving proportion `→ 1/n`, the
   `n`-cycle fraction. Mathlib has `X^{q^n} - X` factoring through irreducibles of degree
   `d | n`; the Möbius inversion is the missing piece.

3. **Higher moments / cycle index.** Prove that the `k`-th factorial moment of the number
   of degree-`1` factors tends to `1` (Poisson(1) limit), the polynomial shadow of the
   fixed-point Poisson law for random permutations. The `k = 1` case is exactly
   `total_root_incidences`; `k = 2` needs the ordered-pair incidence count.

4. **Squarefree density.** Prove `#{monic squarefree degree-n} = q^n - q^{n-1}` for
   `n ≥ 2` (discriminant `≠ 0`), so the non-separable proportion is exactly `1/q` — the
   general-`n` version of `card_double_root`, and the honest reading of the prompt's
   `P(discriminant = 0)` claim.

5. **Chebotarev over `F_q(t)`.** Frame the above as the function-field Chebotarev density
   theorem for `S_n`-covers, connecting to the arithmetic (rather than geometric)
   monodromy that genuinely can be `S_n`.
title: **`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisRoots.lean` — the expected-roots identity.**

# Future Directions — Morphogenesis as Algebraic Geometry

The linear analysis established here recasts the onset of Turing patterns as
conic-section geometry: the number of excited spatial modes is an algebraic degree,
and the boundedness of the background level set separates spots from stripes and
labyrinths. Several bold, testable conjectures follow.

## 1. The genus dictionary

**Conjecture.** For a pattern generated by `k` spatial modes, the background level
set is (generically) a smooth real curve whose complexification has genus at most
`(k−1)(k−2)/2`, and the number of bounded ovals equals the number of distinct spot
families in the pattern.

*The key insight is* that the mode count fixes the degree of the defining polynomial,
and the classical genus–degree formula then caps the topological complexity, turning a
statement about pattern topology into an inequality about polynomial degree.

*Why now?* The degree correspondence for single modes (Chebyshev) is fully in hand,
so the remaining step is purely the theory of real plane curves — a mature subject —
applied to explicitly known low-degree families.

## 2. Sharp mode–degree equality

**Conjecture.** A superposition of `k` modes with a nonzero top harmonic has a level
set of algebraic degree *exactly* `k` in the Chebyshev coordinates, and no
reparametrisation lowers this degree.

*The key insight is* that the leading coefficient of the `k`-th Chebyshev polynomial
is `2^{k-1} ≠ 0`, so the top mode cannot be cancelled by lower ones — degree is a
faithful invariant of mode count.

*Why now?* The exact-degree statement is already proved for a single mode and for the
squared three-mode amplitude; extending it to arbitrary superpositions needs only
leading-term bookkeeping, which is tractable.

## 3. Hexagons are sextics

**Conjecture.** Every hexagonally symmetric two-dimensional Turing pattern has a
background level set defined by a sextic curve invariant under the order-6 dihedral
group, and conversely every such invariant sextic is realised by a three-mode
reaction–diffusion system.

*The key insight is* that three modes reach degree six, and the hexagonal symmetry
group acts on degree-six invariants with exactly the dimension needed to parametrise
the observed patterns.

*Why now?* The degree-six ceiling for three-mode systems is established; the missing
ingredient is an invariant-theory computation of dihedral-invariant sextics, which is
finite-dimensional and explicit.

## 4. Boundedness is a bifurcation invariant

**Conjecture.** Along a reaction–diffusion bifurcation path, the transition from spot
to labyrinth morphology coincides exactly with the moment the defining quadratic form
loses definiteness (its discriminant changes sign), and this transition is detectable
from the reaction kinetics alone.

*The key insight is* that boundedness of a conic level set is controlled by the sign
of the quadratic form's discriminant, so a morphological phase transition is an
algebraic sign change rather than a delicate PDE phenomenon.

*Why now?* We have proved the two endpoints of this transition — definite forms give
bounded spots, indefinite forms give unbounded labyrinths — so the conjecture is the
natural interpolation and is amenable to explicit discriminant tracking.

## 5. Three-dimensional morphogenesis as algebraic surfaces

**Conjecture.** In three spatial dimensions, a `k`-mode Turing pattern has a
background level set that is a real algebraic surface of degree `k`, and the Turing
"gyroid" and "diamond" phases correspond to specific cubic and quartic surfaces.

*The key insight is* that the Chebyshev correspondence is dimension-agnostic: each
axial mode contributes one polynomial degree, so multi-dimensional patterns inherit
the same degree = mode-count law, now for surfaces.

*Why now?* The one-dimensional degree law and the planar conic dichotomy are proved;
lifting to surfaces reuses the same Chebyshev machinery with additional coordinates.

# Future Directions: Homological Quantum Codes

This cycle established the exact dictionary "logical qubits = middle homology"
for the chain-complex model of CSS codes, and used it to compute the logical
dimension of the hypercube homological code, refuting the folklore "one qubit"
law for the hypercube *graph*. The following conjectures extend those findings.

## 1. The distance of the hypercube homological code

**Conjecture.** For the hypercube graph `Qₙ` (`n ≥ 2`), the homological code
`HQECC(Qₙ)` has minimum distance equal to the girth of `Qₙ`, namely `4`,
independent of `n`; consequently it does **not** achieve the quantum Singleton
bound `d = 2^{n/2}` for `n ≥ 5`.

The key insight is that in a one-dimensional complex the shortest nontrivial
cycle is a shortest graph cycle, and every hypercube contains a 4-cycle while
containing no triangle. Distance is therefore a girth invariant, decoupled from
the exponentially large number of encoded qubits computed in this cycle.

Why now? The present cycle pins down the encoded dimension `β₁(Qₙ) = 2ⁿ⁻¹(n−2)+1`
exactly; the natural next parameter is the distance, and the girth heuristic is
directly testable on the same family that already contradicted the qubit count.

## 2. Euler characteristic as a code-rate obstruction

**Conjecture.** For any connected graph complex, the code rate `k/n` of its
homological code equals `1 − (V−1)/E`, and among all connected graphs on a fixed
number of edges the rate is maximized precisely by graphs with a single vertex
of many loops (bouquets) and minimized by trees (rate `0`).

The key insight is that the Euler identity `β₀ − β₁ = V − E`, proved this cycle,
turns the rate into a purely combinatorial ratio; extremizing it is a discrete
isoperimetric problem on the vertex/edge counts.

Why now? The Euler identity was just established in full additive generality over
an arbitrary field, so the rate formula is an immediate corollary awaiting an
extremal analysis.

## 3. Every finite-dimensional homology group is a logical space

**Conjecture.** For every field `K` and every pair of natural numbers `k ≤ n`
there is a length-two chain complex over `K` with middle space of dimension `n`
whose homology has dimension exactly `k`; hence every logical/physical dimension
pair `(k, n)` is realized by some CSS chain complex.

The key insight is that the dimension formula `k = n − rank d₁ − rank d₂` proved
this cycle is not just an inequality but an exact accounting, so realizability
reduces to choosing two maps with prescribed ranks summing to `n − k`.

Why now? With the exact dimension theorem in hand, the realizability question
becomes a rank-prescription problem in linear algebra rather than a homological
mystery.

## 4. Cohomological duality of the two check families

**Conjecture.** For a CSS chain complex the `X`-logical space `ker d₁ / im d₂`
and the `Z`-logical space `ker d₂ᵀ / im d₁ᵀ` have equal dimension, and this common
dimension is a self-dual topological invariant of the complex.

The key insight is that transposition exchanges kernels and cokernels while
preserving ranks, so the dimension formula forces the two homologies to match;
CSS self-duality is thus a shadow of rank symmetry.

Why now? The additive rank-nullity backbone developed this cycle applies verbatim
to the transposed complex, making the duality statement a direct next theorem
rather than a separate development.
title: Exact dictionary "logical qubits = middle homology"

# Future Directions: The Topology and Conservation Laws of Assembled Puzzles

This cycle established a conservation law for jigsaw assemblies — in any validly
assembled row or rectangle the exposed tabs and blanks balance exactly — together
with a boundary-topology reading and an order-two symmetry group governing the
matching relation. The following conjectures push these findings further.

## 1. A conservation law for arbitrary simply connected regions

**Conjecture.** The tab–blank balance holds not only for rectangles but for every
assembly whose footprint is a simply connected region of the square lattice: the
number of exposed tabs equals the number of exposed blanks whenever the outer
boundary consists entirely of flat edges.

The key insight is that the signed edge potential behaves like a discrete
divergence: complementation negates it, so each shared interior edge cancels
against itself, and only the boundary can carry a net charge. A flat boundary
carries none, so the total must vanish regardless of the region's shape.

Why now? The rectangular case is fully settled, and its proof already factors
through purely one-dimensional slices; extending the slicing argument to staircase
and L-shaped footprints is the natural next step and would connect puzzle
assembly to discrete exterior calculus.

## 2. Genus obstructions to assembling a puzzle on a surface

**Conjecture.** If pieces are assembled on a closed surface of genus `g` rather
than on a flat rectangle, the tab–blank balance is corrected by a term determined
solely by `g`: on the torus the balance is exact, while on higher-genus surfaces a
fixed defect appears that cannot be removed by any choice of pieces.

The key insight is that the boundary term in the conservation law is a topological
invariant of the assembly surface; changing the genus changes the way interior
edges can be paired, and the unpaired remainder is forced to match an Euler-
characteristic count.

Why now? The flat conservation law isolates exactly the boundary contribution, so
the same potential can be transported onto quotient surfaces where the boundary is
replaced by identifications — the cleanest possible setting to detect a genus term.

## 3. The symmetry group grows with richer edge alphabets

**Conjecture.** If the edge alphabet is enlarged from three shapes to `2k + 1`
shapes (one self-complementary border shape and `k` complementary tab/blank
pairs), the automorphism group of the interlocking relation is the hyperoctahedral
group of order `2^k · k!`, and its centre is always the single order-two
"flip every interlock" symmetry.

The key insight is that preserving the matching relation is equivalent to
commuting with the complementation involution, and for `k` independent
complementary pairs this centraliser is exactly the group of signed permutations
of the pairs.

Why now? The three-shape case pins the automorphism group at order two and shows
it is generated by the complementation flip; the signed-permutation structure is
already visible there and only needs more pairs to unfold into its full form.

## 4. Assembly hardness survives the conservation constraint

**Conjecture.** Deciding whether a bag of pieces admits a valid rectangular
assembly remains as hard as Boolean satisfiability even when the input is
guaranteed to satisfy the tab–blank balance, so the conservation law — though a
genuine necessary condition — provides no shortcut to a solution.

The key insight is that the reduction from satisfiability can be padded with inert
flat pieces to enforce the balance without changing solvability, showing the
invariant is orthogonal to the combinatorial difficulty.

Why now? With both the reduction and the conservation law in hand, it is finally
possible to ask whether the invariant is a useful filter; the padding argument
suggests it is not, and settling this sharpens the boundary between structure and
hardness in tiling problems.

## 5. Uniqueness of assembly from boundary data

**Conjecture.** For a rectangle whose interior interface shapes are all non-flat, a
valid assembly is rigid: the entire interface pattern is determined by the shapes
exposed along one full row and one full column, so the number of distinct valid
assemblies is at most exponential in the perimeter rather than the area.

The key insight is that each interlocking constraint propagates a shape from one
cell to its neighbour, so boundary data seeds a deterministic fill of the interior
whenever no flat edge interrupts the propagation.

Why now? The interface complementation rule is already known to force each left
edge from its neighbour's right edge; turning this local determinism into a global
counting bound is the immediate combinatorial payoff.
title: Conservation law for jigsaw assemblies — in any validly

# Future Directions — Morphogenesis as Algebraic Geometry

This cycle established the coordinate-free conic classification of two-mode Turing
patterns: the discriminant `Δ = b² − 4ac` of the leading quadratic form decides
whether a pattern's level set is a compact spot (`Δ < 0`) or an unbounded labyrinth
(`Δ > 0`), and the number of active Fourier modes reads off as an exact polynomial
degree that is additive under products and stable under superposition. The following
conjectures push the program toward higher modes, higher dimensions, and genuine
topology.

## 1. The degree–genus law for three-mode flowers

**Conjecture.** A generic three-mode planar pattern is the real locus of a sextic
curve whose smooth complex model has genus `10`, and the number of compact ovals of
the real locus (the visible "spots" of the flower) is bounded by Harnack's count
`g + 1 = 11`; hexagonal spot lattices realize the extremal Harnack curve.

*The key insight is* that mode count controls not just the algebraic degree but the
**genus** of the complexified pattern, so the combinatorics of spot arrangements is
governed by the topology of a Riemann surface rather than by the PDE dynamics.

*Why now?* The exact degree laws for products and superpositions proved in this cycle
give the precise degree of each multi-mode pattern, which is exactly the input Harnack
and Plücker formulas need to convert "number of modes" into "number of ovals."

## 2. Discriminant stability under nonlinear saturation

**Conjecture.** For the full (nonlinear) reaction–diffusion pattern near onset, the
sign of the discriminant of the *linearized* leading form is preserved by the weakly
nonlinear correction: a spot stays a compact component and a labyrinth stays unbounded
for all amplitudes below a computable saturation threshold `A_c`.

*The key insight is* that the bounded/unbounded dichotomy is an **open condition** on
the coefficient vector, so it persists under any sufficiently small deformation — and
the amplitude expansion is exactly such a deformation.

*Why now?* We proved boundedness with an *explicit* radius `4k(a+c)/(4ac−b²)` and
unboundedness with an *explicit* escaping family; both are quantitative enough to
survive a controlled perturbation, turning a qualitative dichotomy into a stability
theorem with an effective threshold.

## 3. Compactness ⇒ finite spot census

**Conjecture.** Whenever the leading form is positive definite, the pattern's level
set is not only compact but carries a finite, computable Euler characteristic, and the
spot count equals `1 + (number of interior critical values crossed)`; the map from
coefficient space to spot count is locally constant away from the discriminant wall
`Δ = 0`.

*The key insight is* that upgrading boundedness to **compactness** (proved this cycle
via Heine–Borel) makes Morse theory available on the level set, so the discrete spot
census becomes a topological invariant rather than a numerical artifact.

*Why now?* Compactness of the anisotropic spot locus is exactly the hypothesis Morse
theory requires; with it in hand, the critical-point count becomes a legitimate
invariant to conjecture about.

## 4. Higher-dimensional morphogenesis and definiteness

**Conjecture.** In three spatial dimensions the spot/tube/lamella trichotomy of a
two-mode pattern is decided by the **signature** of the `3×3` symmetric matrix of the
leading quadratic form: signature `(3,0)` gives compact blobs, `(2,1)` gives unbounded
one-sheeted tubes, and `(1,2)` gives lamellar sheets, with the boundaries exactly the
loci where an eigenvalue vanishes.

*The key insight is* that the planar discriminant is the two-dimensional shadow of the
**inertia (signature)** of the quadratic form, so the entire zoology of 3D
morphologies is a table of eigenvalue-sign patterns.

*Why now?* The planar proofs here were written frame-independently (they never assumed
axis alignment), so they generalize verbatim to the diagonalized higher-dimensional
form once the spectral theorem supplies the eigenbasis.

## 5. Aperiodic flowers from irrational mode ratios

**Conjecture.** A superposition of two modes with irrational frequency ratio produces
a pattern whose level set is a dense, non-algebraic curve, yet every finite truncation
is algebraic of the exact degree given by the higher mode; the "defect" between the
truncation and the limit is quantified by a Diophantine approximation exponent of the
ratio.

*The key insight is* that algebraicity is a **finiteness** phenomenon in mode count,
so irrational mode ratios are precisely the boundary where the algebraic-geometry model
breaks and quasicrystalline order takes over.

*Why now?* The exact superposition-degree law proved this cycle pins the degree of
every rational truncation, giving a rigorous baseline against which the irrational
limit's departure from algebraicity can be measured.
title: Coordinate-free conic classification of two-mode Turi

# Future Directions — Turing's Flowers: Morphogenesis as Algebraic Geometry

The file `Catalog/Novelty/TuringFlowersAlgebraicGeometry.lean` establishes the
degree/Chebyshev correspondence and the boundedness dichotomy that separates the
three linear-onset morphological classes (spots, stripes, labyrinths). Twelve
theorems are proved, all `sorry`-free. Natural next steps:

## 1. Genus from complexification
The strongest form of the guiding conjecture reads pattern topology from the genus of
the complexified projective curve `T_n(X) − c = 0`. Formalizing this needs the theory
of real/complex plane curves (smooth models, genus–degree formula
`g = (d−1)(d−2)/2`, real ovals vs. non-compact branches). This is presently the main
missing piece; Mathlib does not yet carry the genus–degree formula in usable form.

## 2. Exact degree of arbitrary multi-mode superpositions
Show that a superposition `∑_{k=1}^{m} a_k cos(k θ)` with `a_m ≠ 0` is a polynomial of
degree exactly `m` in `X = cos θ` (leading coefficient `2^{m-1} a_m`). This upgrades
`mode_as_poly` from single modes to genuine patterns and pins the algebraic degree to
the highest active mode.

## 3. Two-dimensional level sets and lattices
Extend the 1-D `cos(nx)` analysis to planar modes `cos(k·x)` for wave vectors on a
hexagonal/square lattice, and connect the number of lattice orbits to the algebraic
degree of the resulting real variety (the sextic case corresponds to the classic
hexagonal three-mode instability).

## 4. Sharpness of the ellipse bound
`ellipse_bounded` uses the loose radius `c/a + c/b`. Replace it with the sharp
enclosing radius `√(c/min(a,b))` and prove tightness by exhibiting a point achieving
it, giving a metric characterization of spot size in terms of diffusion anisotropy.

## 5. Periodicity lattice of stripes
`stripe_periodic` records invariance under a single generator `2π`. Formalize the full
translation lattice and the quotient torus, framing a stripe pattern as a function on
`ℝ / 2πℤ` and linking mode count to winding number.

## 6. Link to the PDE
Connect the algebraic level sets back to genuine reaction–diffusion dynamics: derive
the linear dispersion relation, identify the band of unstable wave numbers, and show
that the truncated Fourier expansion at onset lands in the polynomial class studied
here.

# Future Directions — Leading-Term Cancellation and Spectral Balance

The results of this cycle establish that the leading correction to a spectral
heat-kernel trace, `L(t) = Σᵢ dᵢ e^{−t Eᵢ}`, cancels identically exactly when the
diagonal shifts balance within each degenerate energy level. Three structural
ideas emerged: (i) transcendental cancellation is controlled by a Vandermonde
determinant obtained from integer temperature samples; (ii) degeneracy is the
*only* source of nontrivial cancellation; (iii) the level-partition of the
spectrum organizes the whole phenomenon. These suggest the following bold,
falsifiable conjectures.

## Conjecture 1 — Second-order cancellation is governed by off-diagonal balance

The subleading `1/N²` term of the heat-kernel trace cancels identically for all
temperatures if and only if, on each degenerate level, both the diagonal shift
sum vanishes *and* the level-restricted sum of squared off-diagonal couplings
weighted by inverse energy gaps vanishes.

**The key insight is** that once the first-order (diagonal) obstruction is
removed, the next obstruction is a quadratic form in the off-diagonal couplings
whose kernel is again a level-by-level balance condition, mirroring the
first-order structure one rung higher.

**Why now?** The first-order picture is now completely pinned down, including the
exact mechanism (intra-level balance) and the exact failure mode (simple
spectra). This gives a clean base case and a precise notion of "what must already
vanish" before the second-order term can be isolated, making the quadratic
obstruction well-posed for the first time.

## Conjecture 2 — Genericity of non-cancellation

For a fixed spectrum, the set of perturbations whose leading term cancels forms a
proper linear subspace whose codimension equals the number of distinct energy
values. Consequently, cancellation is a measure-zero, non-generic event unless
forced by symmetry.

**The key insight is** that the cancellation locus is precisely the joint kernel
of the "level-sum" functionals, one per distinct eigenvalue, and these
functionals are linearly independent, so the codimension counts the levels
exactly.

**Why now?** The characterization by level sums converts a hard analytic
condition ("vanishes for all t") into a finite linear system, so the dimension
count becomes a concrete, checkable claim rather than a heuristic about
"typical" behavior.

## Conjecture 3 — Symmetry certifies cancellation

If a finite symmetry group acts on the spectrum with the perturbation
transforming in a nontrivial irreducible representation, then every degenerate
level carrying that representation has vanishing diagonal shift sum, so the
leading term cancels automatically.

**The key insight is** that the level-sum functional is the projection onto the
trivial isotypic component, so any perturbation living purely in a nontrivial
representation is annihilated level-by-level without any fine-tuning.

**Why now?** With cancellation reduced to the vanishing of explicit level sums,
the connection to representation theory becomes a direct statement about
characters, turning an accidental-looking analytic identity into a structural
consequence of symmetry.

## Conjecture 4 — Rigidity across temperatures forces rigidity across gaps

If the leading term merely decays faster than every single exponential `e^{−t E_i}`
as `t → ∞` (rather than vanishing identically), then the diagonal shift sum on
the lowest level must already vanish, and the argument cascades upward through the
gaps.

**The key insight is** that the slowest-decaying surviving level dominates the
large-temperature asymptotics, so any anomalously fast decay is impossible unless
that level is already balanced, after which the next level inherits the same
constraint.

**Why now?** The Vandermonde/moment reduction makes the large-`t` dominance
argument fully rigorous, so the intuitive "leading exponential wins" heuristic can
be promoted to an inductive rigidity theorem across the entire gap structure.

# Future Directions: Algebraic Geometry of Neural Decision Boundaries

This cycle established that a rectified-linear classifier's decision boundary is
a *tropical hypersurface*, and that its algebraic complexity is governed by two
exact arithmetic laws of the max-plus algebra: monomial counts **add** under a
rectified-linear activation and **multiply** under composition of independent
units. From these findings we distil the following bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. Exact monomial-count recursion for layered networks

**Conjecture.** For a layered rectified-linear network of depth `L` with layer
widths `w_1, …, w_L`, the number of affine monomials in the numerator of the
computed tropical rational function satisfies the exact recursion
`m_{k+1} = m_k + d_k`, where `d_k` is the current denominator count, and hence is
bounded above by `2^L · ∏_i w_i`; moreover this bound is attained on an open set
of weights.

**The key insight is** that a rectified-linear activation applied to a tropical
rational `p ⊖ q` returns `max(p,q) ⊖ q`, so the numerator's monomial set is the
*disjoint union* of the numerator and denominator sets — turning depth into
addition and width into multiplication of monomial counts.

**Why now?** The two combining laws (union under activation, product under
composition) have been isolated as clean, weight-independent identities, so the
recursion can now be tracked exactly rather than estimated, and the tightness of
the classical `2^L` region bound can be tested layer by layer on trained
networks.

## 2. The singular locus is a codimension-two tropical stratum

**Conjecture.** The non-smooth points of the decision boundary — where three or
more affine pieces meet — form a tropical stratum of codimension two, and their
number is bounded by `∏_i (w_i choose 2)`.

**The key insight is** that a boundary point is singular exactly when the maximum
defining the tropical polynomial is attained by three or more monomials
simultaneously, an incidence condition of the same combinatorial type that
governs the vertices of tropical curves.

**Why now?** Having characterized the boundary as the equalizer `{p = q}` of two
continuous convex tropical polynomials, the singular locus can be described
purely as a multiplicity-of-argmax condition, making the codimension count a
combinatorial question about which monomial families tie.

## 3. Curvature-free certified robustness radius

**Conjecture.** Because each tropical polynomial is convex and piecewise linear,
the certified robustness radius at a correctly classified point equals the
classification margin divided by twice the sum of the two dominant monomial
slopes — with no dependence on any second-order (curvature) term.

**The key insight is** that convexity forces the local Lipschitz constant to be
realized by a single affine piece, so the robustness certificate depends only on
the active monomial's weights, not on the global network.

**Why now?** With convexity and continuity of the tropical value established, the
local-to-global reduction needed for a tight, curvature-free certificate is
available, and can be benchmarked against gradient-based robustness bounds.

## 4. Depth versus width: an addition/multiplication trade-off law

**Conjecture.** At a fixed total monomial budget `B`, the class of decision
boundaries expressible by a depth-`L` width-`w` network is strictly richer when
the budget is spent on depth (`B ≈ 2^L`) than on width (`B ≈ ∏ w_i`), because
addition of monomial families under activation produces non-convex boundaries
unreachable by a single convex tropical polynomial.

**The key insight is** that width alone builds a single convex tropical
polynomial, whereas depth introduces subtraction (`p ⊖ q`) and thus genuine
tropical *rationality*, escaping convexity.

**Why now?** The precise split between the additive (activation) and
multiplicative (composition) growth mechanisms makes the depth/width expressivity
gap a concrete, falsifiable comparison rather than a heuristic slogan.

# Future Directions: Geometry of the Logistic–Tent Conjugacy

This cycle established an exact topological conjugacy between the smooth logistic
map `f(x)=4x(1-x)` and the piecewise-linear tent map `T(t)=1-|2t-1|`, implemented
by the strictly increasing homeomorphism `h(t)=sin²(πt/2)` of the unit interval.
Fixed points, a period-two orbit, and the intertwining of all iterates transfer
verbatim between the two systems. The following conjectures push the same
geometric bridge further.

## 1. Every period is realised, and the count is exponential

**Conjecture.** For each `n ≥ 1` the logistic map has exactly `2ⁿ` points of period
dividing `n` in the unit interval, and it possesses points of *exact* period `n`
for every `n`.

The key insight is that the conjugacy reduces counting logistic periodic points to
counting tent periodic points, and the tent map's `n`-fold iterate is a sawtooth
with `2ⁿ` full ramps, each crossing the diagonal exactly once. Why now? The exact
conjugacy `fⁿ = h ∘ Tⁿ ∘ h⁻¹` and the bijectivity of `h` are already in hand, so
the transcendental fixed-point count for `f` becomes a purely combinatorial count
of sawtooth crossings.

## 2. Density of periodic seeds and topological transitivity

**Conjecture.** The periodic points of the logistic map are dense in `[0,1]`, and
the map is topologically transitive; together with sensitive dependence this
certifies Devaney chaos on the whole interval.

The key insight is that a homeomorphism preserves density and transitivity, so it
suffices to prove them for the tent map, where periodic seeds are the dyadic-type
rationals `k/(2ⁿ±1)` and are manifestly dense. Why now? With `h` proven to be a
homeomorphism, every topological property of the tent map — the transparent model
— transfers directly to the logistic map without any smooth analysis.

## 3. Invariant density and the arcsine law

**Conjecture.** The logistic map preserves the arcsine measure with density
`1 / (π √(x(1-x)))`, which is exactly the pushforward under `h` of the uniform
(Lebesgue) measure preserved by the tent map.

The key insight is that `h` conjugates the uniform-preserving tent map to the
logistic map, so the invariant density of `f` must be the image of the flat density
under the change of variables `x = sin²(πt/2)`, whose Jacobian produces the arcsine
weight. Why now? The explicit, differentiable conjugating map `h` makes the
change-of-variables computation elementary, turning a statement about a smooth
chaotic system into a one-line pushforward of Lebesgue measure.

## 4. Cryptographic fragility is coordinate-independent

**Conjecture.** Any invariant an attacker can compute from a logistic keystream
(bias, autocorrelation, algebraic degree of seed recovery) has an exact tent-map
counterpart obtainable by applying `h⁻¹`; hence the "chaos cipher" offers no
security beyond its piecewise-linear shadow.

The key insight is that a keystream masked by logistic iterates is, in the `h`
coordinate, masked by tent iterates — a binary shift map whose bits are read
directly off the seed. Why now? The exact conjugacy makes "look how complicated
the parabola orbit is" quantifiable: complexity claimed in the smooth coordinate
evaporates in the conjugate linear coordinate, giving a rigorous no-go statement
for logistic-map stream ciphers.

# Future Directions — The 3n+1 Map: Tropical Dynamics and the Logic of Halting

This cycle established the elementary but rigorous scaffolding around the Collatz
map: orbit-invariance of the halting predicate, the exact stopping time of powers
of two, the decidable bounded halting predicate, the precise logical shape of a
refutation, and a min-plus (tropical) recurrence for the total stopping time. The
following conjectures grow directly out of those findings.

## Conjecture 1 — The stopping time is the unique fixed point of a tropical operator

Define, on the min-plus semiring `(ℕ ∪ {∞}, min, +)`, the Bellman operator
`(Φ f)(1) = 0` and `(Φ f)(n) = 1 + f(T n)` for `n ≠ 1`. Then the total stopping
time is the least fixed point of `Φ`, and `Φ` is a contraction in the natural
graph metric on halting orbits.

The key insight is that halting-time functions for the `3n+1` map are exactly the
fixed points of a tropical shortest-path operator, so Collatz becomes a statement
about global reachability in a min-plus dynamical system rather than about integer
arithmetic. Why now? The recurrence `σ(n) = 1 + σ(T n)` is already isolated and
verified here; upgrading it to a uniqueness-of-fixed-point theorem only requires a
well-founded measure on the halting set, which the orbit-invariance lemmas supply.

## Conjecture 2 — No uniform certificate bound is provable in a weak base theory

For each `N`, the statement "every `n ≤ N` reaches `1`" is decidable and provable
by finite search. The conjecture is that there is **no** primitive-recursive
function `B(N)` with a low-complexity proof that every `n ≤ N` halts within `B(N)`
steps; equivalently, the certified stopping-time bound outgrows every provably
total function of the base theory.

The key insight is that the halting predicate factors as a countable union of
decidable bounded predicates with no uniform bound, which is exactly the signature
of a statement whose totality is unprovable in weak arithmetic. Why now? The
decomposition `Reaches n ↔ ∃ b, ReachesWithin b n` is formalized here, pinning the
open content to the growth rate of the bound `b` — the precise quantity an
independence argument must control.

## Conjecture 3 — Collatz is Π₂-complete relative to the accelerated map

Let `T'` be the accelerated (odd-step) map `n ↦ (3n+1)/2`. The conjecture is that
the halting problems for `T` and `T'` are interreducible by primitive-recursive
translations preserving stopping-time parity, so that any independence phenomenon
for one transfers to the other.

The key insight is that acceleration only reparametrizes the orbit graph, leaving
the min-plus reachability structure invariant, so undecidability is a property of
the graph and not of the particular step function. Why now? The orbit-invariance
lemmas (`reaches_iff_collatz`) already show the halting predicate is stable under
single-step reparametrization; extending stability to the accelerated map is the
natural next reduction.

## Conjecture 4 — Cycle exclusion is equivalent to a tropical eigenvalue bound

A nontrivial Collatz cycle would be a closed walk in the orbit graph with net
multiplier `< 1` in the tropical sense. The conjecture is that the absence of such
cycles is equivalent to a strict inequality between the tropical (min-plus)
eigenvalue of the odd-step operator and `0`, giving a spectral criterion for the
cycle half of the conjecture.

The key insight is that cyclic counterexamples are precisely tropical
eigenvectors, so ruling them out is a statement about the min-plus spectrum rather
than about individual integers. Why now? The stopping-time recurrence identifies
the map with a shortest-path operator, and min-plus spectral theory provides exactly
the eigenvalue machinery needed to phrase cycle exclusion.
